BIRTHDAY WISHES What shall I wish thee, Oh! sister mine, . On thy natal day? The merry bird sings thee a melody fine As his birthday,lay;,, 'lllteitufgriig:bee murmurs froniflOiderto,fiowet• his wishes for thee; Then what of my wishes this natal hour, t What shall they be? Shall I wish thee the miser's hoarded store, His treasures of gold? , Shall I wish thee abundance of precious ore ' And riches untold ? , A mansion that stands in a vast estate, Fair, massive, and grand, ; ' Mountain and valley, river and lake, Acres of land? No, for the riches of earth may talge wings • As light as the air; No, for the wealth of the miser brings • - Nothing bnre; No, for,tbe 4oiap of the worn is but vaiß, ' ) And lives but a day; ; No, for its splendours cannot remain For ever and aye. ' • Shall I wish thee a life that is free from care, And knoweth no fears, t Wots not of aneuish, of pain, of despair, All smiles and no tears? Shall I wish thee a life that is bright and fair Like a summer day, No cloud of distress, disappointment, or care Crossing thy way? No, for Gad chasteneth each child of His love t By sorrow and pain, Making him fit for the mansions'aiove With God to reign. ; No, for the Father, as seemeth Him best, ' • Puts griefs in our way, ' And he that o'eccpmeth shall truly be blest • A ifor ever and aye. . Sister, I wish thee joys greater than thie •`' World can afford; 4' • I wish thee a life,full of infinite bliss Given by thy Lord. I wish thee the faith that can conquer all grief, Sorrow, and care, The martyrs' faith that can bring thee relief In the depth of despair.' ; I wish thee a heart that can trust in its God When burdene4 with fear, That bath never a doubt though An•iction's dull rod Is hovering' near; ' A heart that in dreary Adversity's days, Darksome and long, Clinffs closer tar God and still tells forth His praise. ••In heaven-born song. • . And, sister, when God seest fit thee te call From earth's battle aid strife,. • , When thou hast passed the last milestone of all On the highway of life, Grant that thy soul from its fetters set free May joyfully soar To rest in the realms of Eternity With God evermore. Preston. Elceiston.

As time is of all thing the most precious, so mtrst the 'waste of it be the greatest prodigality. All are not taken—there are left - Living lieloveds, tender looks to bring., , And make the daylight still a JaaPPy thing: The great misfortune with Most Of us is we are con- stantly looking ahead for our experience, instead of looking behind. There is a great difference between being in the world and having the world in us. Let a ship be in the water, and it's all right; but let the water be in the ship, and &wit she goes. _ There are men who no more grasp the truth which they seem to hold than a sparrow grasps the message passing through the electric wire on which it perches.— Norma Macleod. Said Miss Louisa M. Alcott recently, when seasick on board an Atlantic steamer: "They name ships Asia and= Persia and Scotia. I wonder why_it doesn't occur to somebody to name one Nausea ?" A photographer in a country town was recently visited , by a young woman, who with sweet simplicity asked, "flow long does it take to have your photograph taken after you have left your measure ?" "Are you papa's boy ?" "Yes, sir." "And are you mamma's boy ?" "Yes, sir." "Rut how can you be papa's boy and mamma's at the same time?" After a pause, "Can't a nice carriage have two horses ?" When men face a duty, not merely, will that duty be- come at once less unpleasant to them. but life itself will immediately begin to gather interett fer in duty, and in duty only, does the individual begin to come into real contact with life; therein only can he see what life is, and grow fit, for it.— Jraodorteld. An old Scotch lady being in London, observed aboy; a currier's shop door a cow's tail fixed to the wall by way of a sign. She stood for a -Considerable time medi- tating on the curious sign. The shopman went out and politely asked her what it was that drew her notice so much, upon which she answered, " stooden an' lookit near an oor at that coo's tail, WI canna see_Prbe name of wonder, boo the coo cud gang in at sic a smas hole and no' be able tae pu' in her tail after her." All substances the cunning chemist, Time, Melts down into that liquor of my life— • Friends, foes, joys, fortunes, beauty, and disgust, - And whether I am angry or content, Indebted or insulted, loved or hurt, All he distils into sidereal wine And brims my little cup; heedless, alas! Of all he sheds, how little it will hold, How much runs over on the desert sands.—Emersess. The young are seldom forbearing, because they so little understand the frailties of poor human native. Oh if you could only witness the terrible struggles i passing n the heart of that friend whose vivacity annoys you, whose fickleness provokes you, whose faults some" times even make you blush. Oh lif you saw the tears ,1 that are shed in secret; the vexation felt against self II (perhaps on your account) you would indeed pity theni. Love them! make allowances for them! never let them feel that you know their failings. To make anyone be- 1 lieve himself good is to help him, almost in spite of self, , .to become so. A correspondent of an exchange relates that he re- cently made a bicycle tour in Jutland; and that, upon a eecond time passing through a small village near Viborg, he was told a story which, for a day or two, had much exercised the minds of the local gossips. On this occa- sion-of. his first visit to the neighbourhood.. the bicyclist was benighted, and, having lighted his lardp, rode at top- most speed for many miles along a lonely highway in the dark. He was seen by a passing countryman, who stricken with terror, fell upon his knees, and was found in that attitude by a belated letter carrier. "What is the matter?" the postman asked. "What, indeed," stammered the peasant, "the devil has just gone by on a windmill." A PAHL EXTORTIONI42.—Miss Chudleigh may be're- garded as the ideal and type of the kg of pert, or even realapert, young ladies:who trete& as maids of honour in the courts of the first two Georges. A good story is told by Charles Knight in his" London," which, whether-it- be true or faise, is at all events characteristic of her transcendent impudence Apa'rtments in Hampton Court Palace having been allotted to her mother, the king good-naturally asked Miss Chudleigh one day bow the old lady felt in her new abode. "Oh, very well, if the poor woman had only a bed to lie upon!" "That oversight Mll3 be repaired," said the king. On thi, hint, the maid of honour (who continued a maid of honour for twenty years after her clandestine marriage with the hon. Mr. Hervey, afterwards Earl of Bristol) acted, and in due time there appeared among the royal household accounts, "To a bed and furniture for the apartments of the Hon. Mrs. Chudleigh, £4,000." The king, -who, though decidedly fond of money, was a man of his word. paid the bill, but remarked that if Mrs. Chudleigh found the bed as hard as he did, she would never sleep in it.— Cassell's " Greater London." A FRENCHMAN.—The common idea of a Frenchman— and the idea is not confined to England—is that he is superficial, frivolous, vain, puerile, immoral, and incon- stant; nothing much at any time, and nothing very long, and invariably in the extreme of whatever he is at. Even Jakob Grimm refused to believe any Frenchman capable of a "sentiment truly moral." Yet it is easy to shew that France has been foremost in every intellectual move- ment in Europe, that if her national literature has a fri- volous side, it has also a serious aspect, so that the stock sarcasms vent efl against the levity and lack of• solidity • ,cbaracteristic of the nation might easily enough be nega- tived by facts which on the surface look quite as cogent RA those in support of the opposite association. Yet, taking the popular opinicn all in all, it is perhaps more accurate than that which would attribute to the French a superiority over every- other nation, and represent them as possessed of an ideal so lofty that while it may be tuned at by some of them, it is assuredly attained by few. The love of ostentrilion, and the fickleness displayed in endless changes of government, may be on one side as- cribed to the eagerness to attain this acme of perfection. On the other hand, the innate vanity and inconstancy of the nation may be set down as the moving cause of these actions. In truth, such conduct as that with which we associate the Frenchman is, tO'a great extent, typical of of the Celt, who appears the Moment we scrape the.tßo- manised Gaul. His intellect is bright, but not capable of any very ponderous effort, his love of change so all per- vaaing, that on the first opportunity for indulging in it he is apt to "'shoot Niagara," without caring or thinking what comes afterwards. Completeness of theory is his curse; utter want of any capacity for "halving the dif- ference," so as to arrive at a modus vimtli, his bane in politics. This, rather than the ingratitude of which he is sometimes accused by critiss of his own people, is what tempts a Frenchman to drift from one form of Govern- ment to another, the superior advantage of which iS not apparent to more prosaic spectators.—" The Peoples of the World" for November. nimllSTlßS—whose professional labours neressitatel long in- tervals between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating, comforting and capable of sustaining exhausted natu 43 as Cadbury's Cocos, gnaranteod absolutely pure..-Advt.

Shores (Liberal agent). .T be ' Chairman, who was greeted with loud" applause, said lee would call upon Mr. Shores to read some letters which bad heen received from gentlemen who were unable to be present that evening. ' 4'Mr. 'Shores then read a considerable number •of letters from Mr. H. Gladstone, Mr. C. M. Percy, and others. The Chairmao, having then announced that an Overflow Meeting would be held at the Baths, said be could con- giatulkite them most sincerely upon being there on • that extremely memorable occasion. Tney had had many.. meetings in that hall before on .political sablects, but they never had one of an interest that attached to the meeting of that night. They were there as they knew to hear an address from their chosen can- didate. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He should like to explain fore =Meat what he meant by that term," chosen candidate."- The' Would remember that before the present Act came into f orce they had a Liberal Association con- nected with Widnes of which their friend Mr. Muspratt was the president. But on the passing of the new Reform Bill into law it became obvious that they ought to commence a new association on, if possible, much more democratic lines than were the older ones. They therefore, at Mr. Muspratt's suggestion, and at the suggestion of several other friends of their associatloo, called the chairmen of the old associations together, and then they called the Liberals of the various districts of which that division of Lancashire was composed ' and the relltilf was that they had now a new Liberal Asso- hialion &Instituted on the most democratic buds that he thoeght,kwas poorible to constitute any association Upon ; and they bad a large council of over 400 membtrs who were elected at public meetings in the various districts by the Liberals of those various districts. (Hear, hear.) The pecu- tliar function of She members of that council was to choose a candidate who should be submitted to the constituency, and that wag what that council had done. Mr. Muspratt's name had been suggested to the councils Of the various dis- tricts, and they had unanimously adopted him as their can- didate for the coming campaign. (Applause.) Alluding to ' the work that the new amociation had already been able to accomplish, be said they would remember that under the Act that had just expired there were about 700 or 800 elec- tors in the polling district of Widnes, which comprised Widnes, Cronten, and Ditton. Now under the new system of things there were 4,000 electors. (Applause) If the people of Widnee could not make their wants ksown through those 4,000 elector, it would be a great pity. (Hear, hear.) This was the point they had to consider: one polling station had done for those 700 or 800 people, but it was perfectly obvious that 4,000 people could not, poll comfortably where 700 could poll. In fact it was utterly ' impossible for the 4,000 electors to poll is that one polling place. (Hear, hear.) The working-men of Widnes were now foe the first time entrusted with the franchise, but' they would either have had to sacrifice half a day's pay, or they would have to sacrifice their dinner hour, or crowd up after their works were closed at six o'clock to register their I choice. There was a committee of magistrates appointed to investigate that question of polling districts, and there was a deputation from their Liberal Association appointed to i wait upon that committee of magistrates. They did so and they took Lord Selisbury'e—(hooting)—advice for once, and they took before the committee a big map, and showed them how impossible it was for the working-men of Widnes to vote at the one polling place. They saw their friend Sir Thomas Brockiebank on that committee of magistrates, and they knew then that their case would be fairly stated. I (Heat, hear.) But be should like to ask where were the local Conservatives en that occasion.. There was not a single representative of the Conservative Association of Widnes to represent the Widnes working-men. (" Shame.' ) The Conservatives were very fond of telling them that they desired the vote for the working-man, and that there were no end of Conservative working-men, but he wanted to know why they were not there to assist the Liberal deputa- tion before the committee of magistrates. (Hear, hear.) Not only were they not there, but Mr. Woodnorth, the Con- servative agent for South-West Division of Lancashire, did all he could to oppose the multiplication of the polling places. ("Shame.") But fortunately, although they (the Liberal deputation) did not get all they wanted, they got double the number of polling places—one at West Bank and another at Sim's Cross. (Applause.) He might tell them that the Liberal Association had placed several hundred electors on tfte voting lists who otherwise would not be en- titled to vote at the next election. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) But from the question of organisation he must proceed to their candidate Mr. Muspratt. (Applause.) Al- luding to the death of Mr. Muspratt's brother he said that they had been told by Mr. Muspratt that in consequence of that lamented event he would be unable to attend a sufficient number of meetings and attend to the details, but they told him that if he would only become their can- didate they would do all the work for hist as far as they possibly could. (Applause.) And they told him that ' ,they could rely upon the electors of Widnes not only haying sympathy with him in his loss, but that they would Show that sympathy by hearty co-operation and by earnest work on his behalf. (Loud applause.) Referring to Mr. Muspratt's political viewe, he said they must bear in mind that those opinions, whatever they were, were not the result of any recent conversion. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He bad ate same views with regard to Ireland, with regard to education, and with regard to the other burning questions that would come, before the Parliament for many years. They had been the result of mature study, and much care- ful thought on his part. (Hear, hear.) Haying glanced at the recent changes of opinion of Lord R. Churchill and other Conservatives, Mr. Carey said he should just like to allude fer a moment to the meeting of the Boundary Corn- miseionere in Liverpool. (Hear, hear.) At that meeting Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss—(hisses)—who is the father of their opponent, the Tory candidate, spoke in the most eon- ' Aemptuous terms, not only of Widnes but of the occupations of Widnes and of everybody connected with the town. He did all he could to prevent that division from being called . after the town which possessed halt the population. He

What. . they had to do,in the next Parliament was to carry out those reforms.which had been alluded' to by Mr. Gladstone' in his manifesto. (Cheers.) In the first place, the Houses ; of Parliament had as they knew, become absolutely incapable of Carrying on the business of the country, and it was neces- sary to devolve a certain portion of that business to assem- ; blies elected by the people. • (Cheers.) With regard to local Government, the Liberals, and Mr. Gladstone particu- ' larly, hed pointed out that it was necessary that the new , councils should be elected by the ratepayers._ (Cheers.) ; It the Tory party bad a majority at the next election, al- though Lord Salisbury might bring in a local self-govern- went bill, there would be some attempt made, as on former . occasions, to introduce non-elected members into the man- ; cite • and if returned m Parliament, that was a thing which be Mr. Maspratt) should oppose tooth and nail. (Cheers, , a Voice "Lord Salisbury is one of the forty thieves," and , laughter.) Mr. Gladstone had said that "In the reform of government the first object to be aimed at, in my judgment, should be to rectify the apportioning of taxation as between , real and personal property, to put an end to the gross injus- tice of charging upon labour through the medium o.! the Consolidated Pend, local burdens which our laws have al- ', ways wisely treated as incident to preperty." He (Mr. Musprett) maintained that the whole question of taxation, , required adjustment. He knew that so far as Imperial , taxation was concerned there were many people who ob- , jected to the payment of the income-tax, and he himself quite understood their objection, because, although in some respects the income-tax was a good tax as compared with the taxes upon the necessaries of life, still it was net a good tax in itself. He believed if they pursued a reasonable and economical policy, that the income-tax, if not abolished, , would be reduced to a very small amount. Nor was he , averse to the proposition made by Mr. Chamberlain— , (cheers)—a proposition which had been characterised by one who would not certainly be considered an out-and-out Radical—Lord Derby—(cheers)—as net containing any new , principle. There was a graduated income-tax at present, , and it is only a %mama whether they carried that gradua- tion further. Abed when the Tories talked about confisca- , tion—and they knew the language which they used upon ; question, of that kind—he said to them, "Don't believe them." (Cheers.) Theirs was simply an endeavour to redress the burden of taxation, which he maintained, not- withstanding the reforms already carried, pressed unduly ; upon the poor as compared with the rich. (Cheers.) Therefore, if he was returned by their suffrages he should ; endeavour to follow out so far as he could the principles of the Financial Reform Association, which went to remove the ; remaining taxes upon tea, upon coffee, upon cocoa, upon silver plate, and a variety of other articles that still remain , subject to a tariff. He would endeavour to remove these and sabetitute, as far as possible, a tax upon wealth and ' property. (Cheers.) What was taxation required for ? It was to meet the expenditure of the country, and he said one of the great aims he should have by him would be to put , a atop as far as he could to such wars as the insane invasion of the Soudau, and to the policy of meddling. (Cheers.) He should give a fair consideration, if • returned, to every , question between employer and employed. He was in favour of Mr. Burt's amendment of the Employers' Liabil- ity Act. He was entirely and unreservedly in favour of it. (Cheers.) On the land question, his views were pretty well known. He would prevent settlements on unborn children, and make the land free in every way and as saleable as it , possibly can be made, and that is very nearly as saleable as Consols or railway stock. Even if they freed the sale of the land there remaived the question of freedom of cultiva- tion, and there would be none until the laws were amended. The laws required amending in the direetion advo- eated by Professor Sheldon, the candidate for Orm- skirit Division. (Cheers.) He advocated full security to every tenaet for the capital he put in the land. (Cheers.) There came another question, and that was a question which had fluttered the dovecote of Liberalism—he meant Mr. Chamberlain's suggestion to give compulsory powers to the new county councils for the purchase of land for the purposes of allotments. That question was a very new one. Ile twain agreed with Lord Derby that there was nothing confiscatory about it. The only question at to which there would be awe division of opinion was as to the means of carrying it out, and on that he reserved his judgment for the present. (Cheers.) Upon the question of education he. said in his address, "If we are to meet successfully the cow-" petition of other nations in manufacturing industry, our system of education, both primary and secondary, must be improved. As one of the main causes of irregularity of at- tendance in primary schools is the payment of school fees, ' I hope to see them abolished; and lam of opinion this can be done without injury, and indeed with benefit in poor districts, to voluntary or denominational schools, by means of an increased grant from the Consolidated Fund, and without interfering with the present management." (Cheers.) I am glad to see that Cardinal Manning— ' (cheers)—himself said, " The ,Catholic Church is not against free education ; in fact the Catholic Church has always been in favour of free education." (Cheers.) .And when he considered the great labour of the Catholic clergy amongst the poor, what they were doing constantly in their interests, he could not but believe that, provided they were satisfied that their religion would not be interfered with in any way, the Catholics would be in favour of free education. (Cheers.) If, as at the Widnes School Board, Roman Catholics, Churcbmen, and Dissenters could meet to- gether and discuss educational questions amicably, was it not a sign that by a little forbearance on the part of many people they should be able to attain that great end without injuring the Catholics in any way. (Cheers.) He was in- formed of the great difficulties under which some schools at present labour. He was informed that in Father Finegan's schools at Appleton, owing to good management and an ex- cellent teaching staff, they had during the past twelve months earned 20s 2d per head; but owing to the 114th clause of the Education Act, a larger grant cannot be made than 17s 6d per head anless the fees and subscriptions are equal in amount to the increased grant. ("Shame") That was an injustice which ought to be done away with; and the sooner the better. (Cheers.) He was also informed

• FIITERAt—DEMONSTR-ATION AT wmatinfxon, PEEtiIIES OF MR. S. SMITH, M.P., MR. W. CROSFIELD, AND 'COLONEL MCCOILQUODALB. A highly successful• Liberal demonstration in sup- port of the candidature Of Mr. W. Crosfield, • for Warrington, and Colonel McCorquodale; for New- ton Division, was held itt the Public Hail, Warring- ton; on, Wednesday evening, ,The hall was crowded a considerable time before the meeting commenced, and the utmost enthusiasm prevailed throtigrhotit. The audience wiled away the time by, singing elec- tion dot). songs, under the leadership of ,Mr. Geo. Wal- lingtbo, the local allusions being applauded. An ovsrflow meeting -was also held in the Co-opera- tive Hall. The chair was taken by Mr. J. G. McMin- nies, M.P., who was supported on the platform by Mr: S.' Smith, M.P. (Liverpool), Colonel McCorquo- dale, J.P., Mr. W. Crosfield, J.P., Alderman Crosfield, J.l' Alderman Burgess J.P., Alderman Holmes, J.P., Dr. Gornall, J.P. and Messrs. John Rylands, J.P., A. C. McCorquociale, J.P, J. Greening, J.P., E, J. Guest, J.P.; Rev:R. Filcher, 8.A., Rev. J..Yonge, Rev. A. Kenworthy, Rev. J. Calirert, Rev. Howell Jones, and others. The CHAIRMAN, who had a cordial reception, said be was sure he need not say that be was very glad to see that magnificent meeting, and he looked upon it as an augury of their success in the Newton and Warrington Divisions. (Hear, hear.) He kaew a good-Teal" of what was going on in both districts, and he knew a good deal of what was going on previous to the election of 1880. —(hear, hear,)—and he could say with the utinast truthful- ness that from what he knew of their prospects of slimes at the present time that he was perfectly confident that they were 'going to time, as well as. or better, than they did in 188 Q. (Loudebeers.) He daresay they would hear day by day from the,otlaer aide, confident predictions that the- Tories were going to beat them. Don't believe it. (Laugh- ter .and cheers.) They taeard all that en 1880—(laeghter) —and they knew what the reedit was. • Otehetted laugh- ter.) They won, and he knew they would win, bat, he did not know that they woald win by so magnificent a majority as they did on that occasion. (A voice: "A thousand next. time," and cheers) He hoped so, and it was that interjection mat led him to say Oat they must win by a decisive majority. (Hear, hear) Let them put New, on Division of the county, and Warrington, in the position of being secure in the future as etrongholds of Liberalism, invincible and impregnable. (Loud cheers.) Colonel MCCootatronato, who was received with loud applauseettaid he hoped the.chairman's predictions as to the present election would be equally correct with those of 1880. , (Hier, hear.) They had it in their own hands in a great measure, and if they put their shoulders to the wheel there was no doubt whatever, in his opinion, that they would find their labours crowned with success. cHear, hear.) They must rally round the" Grand Old Man ' —(cheers)— who had again and again led them me to victory. (Hear, bear.) They must look to the records of the two millions of sturdy Britons who were marching this month, as it were, to the poll, to discharge the duty that the country had placed in :heir hands, and he had no doubt that they would discharge that duty conscientiously and in favour of the party who obtained the privilege for them—(hear, , heal )—and as a birthright for generations to come here- after. He believed the great bulk of these new electors would record their votes for the party of justice, freedom, land progress. (Applause.) There Was a frightful want of truthfulness in the speeches of some of the candidate who were now seeking fer Parliamentary honours. (Hear, I hear) The Tories were endeavotiring to persuade the peo- ple that they were instrumental in getting the Franchise Bill for them—(" It's a lie ")--but the people, by the daily press given years ago, were able to read the speeches and become acquainted with what bad been said and done in Parliament, and they knew full well that the Tories did not leave one stone un- turned in their endeavours to prevent the passing of the Franchise Bill through the House of Comueons. (Cheers.) The Tories, too, had got the cry ," Church in danger " (laughter)—and it appeared to him that their object was to divert the attention of the new electors from thoee matters Which more immediately concerned them—(bear, hear)—by making them.believe the Church was in danger. (A voice: " Let it fall." Hear, hear. Another voice: 4. tiers beef and less bishops." Loud laughter, and cheers.) The Tories Pro- fessed to support the Established Church, and they looked upon members of the Church who happened to be Liberate as desirous to destroy the Church. In that the Tory party: were acting a very improper part. (Cheers.) By their action in bringing the subject forward were they not leading, towards the disestablishment which they professed to be contrary to . their wishes ? (Bear, hear.) If their object was to make immediate gain for themselves—to be succestif at in the I contest for seats in Parliament, then it was by no means to be recommended or applauded. (Hear, hear.) The men- tion of Sir R. A. Cross's opposition to the Franchise Bill was received with hooting. and cries of "He'll never go again," and "McCorquodale will win.") Sir R. A. Cross, for the consideration of the Newton Division, bad spoken of the enormous expense of the Liberal Govern- ment in spending one hundred millions during the last year, but he did not tell them that the, Liberal Government had to take'a frightful legacy from the other side. (Hear, hear.) Take Afghanistan, where the Tories commenced a troubloue war, which they said would cost about six mil- lions. Then the Liberals came into office, and they had to provide 111 millions more than this sum, for the expendi- ture was 171 millions. (Hear, hear.) That formed part of the enormous expenditure of the Liberal Government, and, that was not all. (Hear, hear.) Sir R. A. Cross forgot to tell his audience that in nine years the Liberal Government paid off 80 millions of the National Debt, and during a similar period the Tories reduced the debt by 2i millions only. (Hear, hear.) He thought that an accusation made by a prominent member of one party should be faithfully 'true in every respect, and not exaggerated one way or the other. (Hear, hear.) Referring to his (the speaker's) ad- dress, Colonel McCorquodale said he did not hesitate Ito state that he cheerfully, and by conviction, adhered to the four points which were laid down in such wonderfully clear language by Mr. Gladstone. Speaking of the three acres and a cow proposal, he said it existed only in the imaginations of the Tories. But he did not see why the ,labouring men of this country should not have power of look- ing forward to the time when they might acquire at a fair and reasonable price a plot of land on which to build a cottage and have a garden when old age crept on, and not as at present, when they quitted their employment, have I frequently to go fin the over crowded towns, and they and I their wives and families inhale the comparetivelv impure air compared to that which they had enjoyed in the coun- try. (Hear, hear.) He referred to the improvement that had taken place in the condition of the farm labourers and the working classes generally during the last fifty years, and, alluding to the proposed County Boards, said they would relieve Parliament of an enormous amount of local business. They would, he believed, also deal with licensing matters, which were at present in an unsatisfac- tory state—(cheers)—and settle them to the greater satisfac- tion of the inhabitants and all concerned than had hitherto been the case. (Cheer's.) He predicted that the labours of the "fair trade commission " would be thrown away'— that there would be no result whatever to help ue. (Hear, hear.) The idea of bolding a Parliamentary inquiry to show a man how to manage his own business! (Cheers.) He pointed to the immense increase in the wealth of the Country since the introduction of free trade, and concluded by saying the electors would .poll according to their con sciences, and for the'man that would discharge his duty the beet. (Loud cheers.) Mr. Wn. An extraordinary dispute between medical men, and one in which, it is etated, the decision affects several hundred cases, was heard before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge, at i the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday. The case had I been brought as a test case, and considerable interest seemed to be excited in it. Dr. Bernard Rifleman, of George-street, sued Frederick Hargreaves for 5s for professional services rendered. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for plaintiff, who stated that he was a member of the Royal College of Sur- geons, and at present attached to the Royal Marines. The amount charged to defendant was fair and reasonable.—De- fendant said he disputed his liability in consequence of a ' notice he received from Mr. Wilson, with whom plaintiff was at the time the debt was contracted, and in consequence of notices which had appeared in a local paper. They were as follows:—" Notice. Dr. Hiffernan begs to inform the public of St. Helens that he has no further connection with Mr Wilsm, of Hall-street. and haa removed to 18, George- street, St. Helens. All persons owing for medicine and at- tendance are requested to pay the same only to Dr. Hiffer- nan." A counter notice was as follows :--.' Mr. Wilson begs to inform the public of St. Helens that Dr. Hiffernan has no right whatever to claim payment to him of bills ' owing to Mr. Wilson, in which he never had any interest, 1 being only a weekly servant at stated wages, which were I regularly paid to hint up to tke time of his discharge. Mr. Wileon further begs to give notice that should Dr. Iliffer- ,nan after this notice receive or claim payment of such bills the will be proceeded against with the utmost rigour of the ' aw."—His Honour asked what defendant had to say on *tie merits of the case.—Defendant said he would call Dr. G Keeffe and Mr. Wilson to give evidence.—Plaintiff eaid he knew no reason for Dr. O'Keeffe coming between them. Ile himself was never engaged as an assistant. —AN agreement which purported to have been entered into between Dr. Hiffernan and Mr. Wil- son was here handed to his honour. Mr. Riley said the agreement was very peculiar in its form. It ap- peared that they agreed to practice jointly; bat Rifleman alone wae on the medical register, and alone entitled to sue. Defendant could net set up that there ought to have been two plaintiffs instead of one.—His Honour : Certainly not.—Mr. Riley continued to say that there was a 'special agreement that Dr. Hiffernan was to prove the debts in the County Court, no doubt to meet the difficulty of Wilson not being qualified so to do.—Mr. Wilson was then called, and 1 he said Dr. O'Keeffe sent defendant the notice about pay- ' ment ; and he (witness) advertised in the papers under legal advice. In reply to Mr. Riley, he said he had no surgical or medical qualifi- cations, and when he entered into that agreement he knew he could not sae for medical services rendered.— Dr. O'Keeffe, examined, said he practised in Widnes. In June, 182. he established a practice in St. Holens.—His Honour: Had you any connection with Dr. Hiffernan ? Witness : Nothing at all; I had nothing to do with him. I established it to be kept for a nephew of mine until he got Qualified. The practice was mine, and I instructed Mr. Wilson to advertise for a duly qualified man to assist him. —His Honour : You could not qualify Mr. Wilson to enter into partnership with a medical man. I give judgment for nlaintiff.

SMITH, X A., SchoLlx of St. John's College, Cambridge; And five Assistant Masters. The Bakool contains two divisions. Toe work of the Lower Division eomprises a regular comae of instruction in English, French, the rudiments of Latin, elementary Mathematics and Science, with Reading, Writing, Arithmetic, Drawing, Drill, and Vocal Music, and all other elements of a sound modern education. fetish worshipper ? He possesses courage, we grmt, but he has not in this instance the courage of his convictions. The, argument oSed both by Mr. DAVIES and Mr. WOODS in favour of a change in the fiscal policy of the country was that there was depression in trade; but the answer is that, admitting there is depression, the depression is greater ,h 1 Protectionist countries. What then ? -If we are hot in the frying pan, shall we ~,cool ourselves by jumping into the fire? Mr. woons seems to think it a bad thing that America is pouring into this country "corn, flour, anton, &c., to-day to the tune of 8.5,000,000 per annum ; " but we would put :t to any working-man whether he can bring uimselt to believe that this country would be better off if, by putting a tax on "corn, fl°or, cotton, &c.,' we increased the cost of these.l,„ articles and lessened the import? uere is not much wisdom, surely, in cutting Off the nose in order to spite the face. Let those who may be hoping that a Tory Govern- rnent will be able to improve upon Liberal a: drniniStration carefully consider the follow- .l,,ng facts, which we take from a speech of BA.ur..ow, the Liberal candidate for the ;Anutsford Division of Cheshire. At a meet- 411Z last week, at Preston, Brook, he said: The trade of the country was very much better While the Liberals were in office than during the Lre:fous five years of Tory rule. Taking the whole Cr of the country, there were during the five anlaeral years nearly 400 millions more of exports iMports than there were in the Conservative 1,0—`,,e• (Cheers.) Ile was afraid that the trade was parried on at a very large percentage of profit, tat it was carried on, and it provided employment for the people of the nation. Never in the history of or cotton trade had there been so large an amount th Wages paid to the operatives in Lancashire as -There was during the last five years. (Cheers.) at "e were were seven million tons of iron and el exported more than in the previous five years. L:,ere was one thing in which the Tories beat the oin)erals, and that was in the number of bankrupt- (Loud laughter, and cheers.) They had 9,000 re bankruptcies in those five years of office than 444 the Liberals in theirs. (Laughter.) ,Sir GILBERT GREENALL must have felt, Zaen Alderman DAVIES, was speaking, that ; was getting it rather hot, as a convert to tee Trade. But he did not venture to reply; he had his mind upon another matter, lor when he got on his feet he WAS, like AJAX, I ready to defy the r lightning. Here is a t.hunderbott which, w understand, was hurled lu our direction :—" I defy the Liberals—l Ell them (Applause) Radicals—l defy the Radicals of n to talk me down or frighten me. and jiPT alle.) They will never 'do it, my friends, 4 tell you why—you won't let them. (Loud- laughter.)" No wonder the laughter Vas loud at the playful chatter of " the frivo- .!°_lls 'Tung thing ; " it must have been as good 1/1 & Nay. As for talking Sir GILTIERT downs that f - • S ft wort. Of supeieiOgation ; the Walton °_ cto.genarian does that more effectually than anything else, whenever he opens his mouth. iis candid friends make remarks, after listening to his speeches—th y use bad Words; they think it is hard on the Conservative party that they should be saddled with such a candidate. After delivering himself of his defiance, Sir GILBERT went on to refer to a handbill ex- osing his hatred to Ireland as shown by his did votes on Irish questions. He F.i,d not like the colour of the bill ; he es " orange" better than "green ;" for buj it was "a shabby piece of paper," • t 'le wouldn't tear it up as that would be vii?° good treatmeqt.” Perhaps Irishmen ..0 ?Member this when they are asked, as a•:.eY are being asked, to vote for the can- tdate who has shown by his conduct in the el'ast that he dispises both them and their 89,1°,14. It is scarcely to the purpose for ‘JILBERT to say of these anti-Irish votes Wr he doesn't remember giving them. is t is it that he does remember? Nor " sufficient to turn mound and say "Sup.t otl did give them, I was wrong, and heun pardon." We do not say that when a._ 18 on his knees to Irishmen, one minute t • ier insulting them, he is not to be pardoned. • We do say that he is not to be trusted. flce bitten they will be twice shy.

The Liberals are fortunate in having such a candidate as Mr. E. K. MIISPRATT, President o,f the Financial Reform Association and president, too, ofthe Society of the Chemical Industries. div.p: Town Councils without reference to the ratepayers. As might be expected, he ex- posed the hollowness of the Tory system of throwing local taxation, upon the Consoli- dated Fund, showing very clearly that property owners were, in this way, being relieved at the expense of every other class, and particularly the working class, who contributed more than their fair share of the Imperial taxes. He agrees with the Trades Union Congress as to the need of reform in the labour laws, and it need hardly be said that he is in favour of Mr. BURT'S Amendment of the Employers' Liability Act. As a member of the Free Land League, Mr. MUSPRATT would, if returned to Parliament. do all in his power to get rid of the evils of entail and of primogeniture. He would cheapen transfer so that land could be bought and sold without difficulty, thus opening it out to capitalists great and small, and thereby relieving the congestion in the labour market. Mr. MUSPRATT is anxious to promote the spread of scientific education, and, while aim- ing at making primary education free, he would seek to remove the disabilities of which the managers of voluntary schools at present complain. Believing in self-government, he would "grant to Ireland as much Home Rule as possible ; " and for the same reason he would_give the control of the liquor traffic to County Boards elected by the ratepayers. Briefly stated, Mr. MUSPRATT'S political creed is—" Government of the people, for the people, and by the people." He is a strong candidate ; the Liberals are strong in the Division; and if they combine to work as they have begun, they will return him by a large majority as member for the Widnes Division of South-West Lancashire.

, ST. HELENS will for the first time be repre- sented in Parliament after the forth-coming General Election; and there will be a keen contest as to who shall have the honour of being the first member of Parliament for the borough. The Liberals are to be congratu- lated on having induced Colonel GAMBLE to champion their cause. He knows the town from end to end, for he is a part of its history. He served it as a Commissioner; he took part in the movement for its incorporation; he was the first Mayor of the borough; he has served it ever since; and we venture to say that it will be a discredit to. the inhabitants if he is not called upon to serve the town as its representative in the new House of Com- mons. Mr. SETON-KARR, the Conservative candidate, has no such personal claims; he is somebec4' dropped from the clouds. He ,! • • man but may be a very " prang • youti6" he is not like c9l9nel GAMBLE; there is no knowing from his past what his "perform- ance" will be. If he wants to start fair, he should retire on this occasion, and come again when he has given hostages as to char- acter in the shape of forty years of public ser- vice in the town that he desires to represent. Both candidates have issued their Addresses; and they are as different as the men. That of Colonel GAMBLE is the staid, thoughtful production of a man of character and of pur- pose, who knows precisely what he is aiming at, and shows himself in quick sympathy with the people; that of Mr. SETON-KARR is juvenile and jejune; it is flighty and bombas- tic, and patronises the Constitution in the style of "a Penny Dreadful." Colonel GAM- BLE'S address goes over a wide range of topics, and it is due to him to point out that there is nothing in what he says of ' "uncertain sound." He does not, like his 1

opponent, talk vaguely about possibly making "such alterations in our Fiscal Policy as may be deemed wise and necessary ; ' he goes straight to the mark by declaring him- self to be "an unflinching Free Trader." Colonel GAMBLE, with a view to getting business done, is "in favour first of all of re- forming the procedure of the House of Com- mons itself.' Mr. SETON-KARR has nothing to say on the subject; perhaps he wishes it to be understood that, like many other Tories, he does not wish to see any business done, and regards obstruction as "constitutional." With regard to "freeing the land," Colonel GAMBLE would "rigorously restrict" entails, abolish the custom of primogeniture, and " endeavour to make the transfer of land as simple and as inexpensive as the transfer of Government Stock." Mr. SETON - KARR, curiously enough for a "constitutionalist," declares himself in favour of land-law reform, but it will be for the electors to consider whether the party—the land-holding party— with which he is allied will be likely to intro- duce reforms which will strike at the root of the privileges of the aristocracy. Colonel GAMBLE would require that the owners of land should take their fair share of the burden of taxation; but Mr. SETON-KARR would make bad worse, for he has the hardi- hood to talk of relieving " real," that is, landed property, at the expense, we suppose, of the industrial and middle classes. Colonel GAMBLE, as an Irishman, denounces Castle Rule.; and we do not doubt that the Irishmen of St. Helens will be better able to trust him than a representative of the party which, if, history is to be relied on, caress when out of office in order that they may kick when they get into power. We have previously pointed out that Mr. SETON-KARR talks childishly as to the cost of Free Education. He is indeed an infant besides Colonel GAMBLE, who is admirably qualified by natural ability, ripe experience, and sterling character to make a representative of whom every inhabitant of St. Helens may well feel proud.

WIDNES C.E.T.S.—The Rev. P. H. Wilson en Thursday delivered a lecture to the members of this society, entitled "Rambles in Scotland." PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE, Ruscoux.—The fortnightly meeting was held on Thursday evening, under the presidency of Mr. J. Ashley. An interesting programme was gone through. THE Rusicotor GYMNASIUM.—The committee of the Y.M.C.A, have requested Mr. Alexander, director of the Liverpool Gymnasium, who has undertaken to be teacher, to open the Gymnasium, at the Drill Hall, by an assault-at- arms, open to the public, at an early date. BETHESDA MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN. —On Wednesday the above society devoted the evening to literature. The attendance was good, and the following' gentlemen gave readings, recitations, ikc. :—Messrs. W. Millington, A. E Jenes4R. Edwards, J. D. Jones, J. Aiken. bead, W. Lacey, Machin, T. Lydiate, and A. Higgins. THE FAILURE OF A WIDNES GROCER.—AI the Liver- pool Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, the public examina- tion of Joseph Matt, grocer, who carried OD business in Widnes and Runcorn, was further Adjourned until the 19th November, so Chat the official receiver might investigate and examine the accounts which the debtor bad Sled the previous day. METHODIST FREE CHURCH BAND OF ROPE. WIDNES.— The members of this society commenced the season on Mon- day evening. about 150 of the young people were given a good tea, and later about 100 adults sat down to tea. Sub- sequently an interesting entertainment of songs, readings, and recitations took place. Mr. E. Gandy, of Runcorn, took the chair. HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—A paper has been read by Mr. T. Millington, of Runcorn, on the "Land .Question." A very interesting evening was passed, and an animated discussion took place, in which Messrs. J. IL Gamon, S. Saunders, W. Rowe, T. Page, and others took part. The Rev. A. P. Watson presided. We are glad to say the meeting was very largely attended by ladies. , ACCIDENT AT A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORIES.—On Tues- day evening a large vitriol chamber, containing about 100 tons of acid, partially collapsed at the works of Messrs. Hut- chinson and Co. Having been in use a considerable period the woodwork had become charred, and one of the cross- bars gave way, the top of the cnamber fell in, and knocked a hole in the bottom. A large quantity of the acid escaped. The damage is estimated about £5O. LIBERAL MEETING AT HELSBY.—An enthusiastic meet-. lug in support of Mr. Lawrence Irweli, the Liberal candi- date for the Eddisbury Division, was held at Helsby on Monday evening. Mr. Thorne presided, and in addition to the candidate speeches were made by Mr. C. Reynolds, J.P., Mr. F. Rigby, J.P., and Mr. B. Kniveton. A resolu- tion to use all legitimate efforts to return Mr. Irwell at the head of the poll was passed unanimously. SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT AT HALEWOOD —Samuel Laird, coatractor, and William Barlow were upon a scaffold at a house they were engaged in building for Lord Derby at Halewood, and about to place a window sill in its position when the plank upon which they were standing gave way. They were precipitated to the ground. and both sustained very serious injuries. After beingexamined by Mr. Richards, aesistant to Dr. McDonnell, of Widnes, they were conveyed to the Liverpool Infirmary. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS, WIDNES. The annual sermons in aid of these missions were preached in the Hart- land-street Chapel, on Sunday last. On Monday evening a public meeting was held in the chapel under the presi- dency of Mr. P. Rawiinson. There was a good audience The Chairman, the Revs. R. Burdon, J. Hothersall, G. Wood (superintendent of the Runcorn circuit). and Mr. Joseph Robinson delivered addresses upon missionary enter- prise. The collections amounted to £7 103 10J. 1.0.G.T, pmts.— The Samaritan Lodge held its weekly meeting on Monday' lvt. The following brothers and sisters were elected oflicere tor•Wic.T, Bro. Wright, W.V.T. Sister Buckley, P.W.C.T. Bro. Machid, Bro. Jones, W.F.S. Bro. Tomlinson, W.Tr. Sister Webb, W.C. Sister A. Lamb, W M. Bro. G. Widders, W.J.G. Bro. D. Widders, W.St. Bro. Harrison, W.A.S. Sister Pearson, W. DM. Sister He.'wn. The ceremony of installation was Perforthed by Bro. Webb, D.G.W.C.T. OnatacictsM air lillti'atuN A WENS.—The "Peace with Honour" Orange Lodge of Runcorn celebrated toe anniversary of the Guy Fawkes Conspiracy on Thursday by a tea party and public meeting in Bethesda schoolroom. Bro. Attewell. of Widnes, presided, and the Rev. W. Pres- ton and Bro. Foley, delivered addresses. A programme of songs, was gone through.—At Widnes, tne Orange Lodge had arranged a bill, which took place at the Drill Hall. About 75 persons were present. cAlgiliT HEDLUND/IP AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, On Thursday, before Captain C. W. Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handley, John Johnson, a tailor out of employ- ment, was charged with stealing a pair of bOots from the shop of Messrs. C. Munsey and Co., High-street. The boots were hanging in the doorway. The manager SAW the pi. saner take them from a nail and make off with them. P.C. Millington went in pursuit, and caught the prisoner with shoes under his coat.—He was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.—On Wednesday morning, a brake van and eleven wagons laden with salt were by some unaccountable means put in motion on the branch line to Weston Point, where they had been left over- night. The line has a very steep gradient, and the wagons attained a great rate of speed. Upon arriving at the em- bankment near Weston Point,the wagonscollided with several other wagons, and there was a tremendous crash. Several were splashed to splinters, and others were hurled to the river wall. Means. Simpson, Davies and Company, and the Cheshire Amalgamated Salt Davies, owned the wagons. A Don's ADVENTURE AT Dirrote.—A young lady, of Hale, travelled from tialebank to Ditcon by the train arriv- ing at the latter station at 3-18 on Wednesday. A hand- some terrier dog had followed her without her knowledge, and it attempted to jump into the carriage as the train was starting, but failed. Those in the carriage thought the animal bad been cut to pieces beneath the wheels of the carriage, but their astonishment was great when on arriving at Ditton Mr. Smith, the station master, found hint clinging in a great state of alarm to the couplings of the carriage. He was quickly reecned from his dangerous positimt and . .
restored.to hie mistress. HALTON AND WESTON POINT.—A public meeting in con- nection with the Wesleyan Missionary Society was held on . .

Tuesday night in the Wesleyan chapel, Haßoca. Mr. Alfred Davies was in the chair. The report was read by the Rev, A. P. Watson. Addressee were delivered by the Revs. Geo. Wood and Simpson Johnson. On Wednesday night a simi- lar meeting was held in the Wesleyan chapel, Weston. The chair was occupied by Mr. James Ford. The report, which was read by Mr. T. Slmister, showed an increase of £4 over last year. An address RAS delivered by the Rev. A. P. Watson on " Our missions in Europe." The Rev. George Wood also addressed the meeting on "The obligation of the church to sustain missionary operations." Cowan" AT BETHESDA SCHOOL, RIINCOIIN.—In con- nection with Bethesda Congregational Chapel, the first of a series of fortnightly pleasant evenings took place on Tues- day evening, when a fair audience gathered. The Rev. J. D. Thome. the poster, presided. The following excellent programme was gone through :—Sorig, "Cleansing Fires," Miss Rhodes; pianoforte solo, Miss Edith Crosby ; recita- tion, "In the Signal Box." Mr. E. J. Rhodes; stump ora- tion on "The Franchise Bill," Mr. A. S. liawkins ; cornet solo, Mr. J. Woods; song, "A Village Story," Miss N. Hand- ley; pianoforte solo, "Oh, dear, what can the matter be ?" Mies Ringland ; song, with violoncello obligato," The Chord of Love," Miss Simkin and Mr. W. Simliin ; song, "The Maid of Argyle," Mr. George Lacy; recitation, " Jud Brownin's Account of Rubenstein'n Playing," Mr. E. J. Rhodes; song," When the flowing Tide comas in." Miss Wright; song, " When the bloom is on the Rye," Mr. C. Powriall. The encores were numerous and deserved, and an

enjoyable time was spent. A Rosana; Puisuces Ftwitn.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions. on Monday, before Mr. James Reynolds and Captain C. W. Dazlehurat, James Payne, landlord of the Cornwall and Devonshire Arms Inn, Church-street, was summoned for refusing to allow P.S. Walley to search the premises. On the 7th all. P.S. Walley and P.C. Finney about ten minutes to midnight heard a noise in the kitchen of the house. They watched the place until twenty minutes te one when they maw a man and a woman of bad character named Annie Williams, who !byes in King-street, go into the yard and shortly afterwards re-enter the house. At half-past one, baying kept a close watch all the time, the officers knocked at the door, and were admitted to the house.'ln the kitchen were three men, apparently sailors, and on the table was a jug full of beer and a number.of glasses. They searched all the rooms downstairs and P.S. Walley was

about to go upstairs, ;ben Mrs. Payne, who appea;ed to answer the summons, locked the door leading to the bed- room and standing with her back against it, ref need to allow him to proceed. The Sergeant informed the Bench that the bowie was -little better than a place of ill-fame.—The defendent was fined 40s and costs, 1.4 s 441. or a month. ASEAELTS ON THE POLICE AT WIG/POS.—At the Widnes Police Court on Monday., before Messrs. F. 'H. Gossage and Holbrook Gaskell, jun., a rough looking fellow named John Doyle was charged with being drank and disorderly, and with assaulting Police-constable Porter. At half-past ten o'clock on Saturday night Porter found the prisoner fight- ing in Pool-street. On being taken into custody prisoner ' became very violent, threw the constable down, and tore his trowsers. The assistance of other constables had to be ob- tained tto convey him to the station. The prisoner, who made his tenth appearance, was fined 10s and costs, or 14 days imprisonment for being drunk, and 6a fine and 64 6d damage and costs for the assault upon the constable, or a further period of 14 days' imprisonment—Joseph Patten was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and with as- saulting Police-constable Holbrook. The constable stated that on Saturday night be saw the prisoner drunk and dis- orderly in Victoria-road. He had been "chucked" out of Andereon'e Commercial Hotel. Witness requested prisoner to go home, and as he refused to do so, he was taken into custody. Prisoner then kicked witness severely on the legs, and one kick which he received on the cap of the knee had since incapaci".ted hint from duty. Police- constable Bowerbank corroborated. Prisoner was fined 5s and costs for bein4 drunk, or seven days' imprisonment, and lOs and costs for the assault on the constable, or 14 days' hard labour. GUNPOWDRH STORE AT WESTON.—The Runcorn magis- trates on Monoay granted Messrs. James and Thomas Handley a license to store gunpowder at Weston. RUNCORN PUBLICANS ON THIS MC/Vt.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Semuel Price was granted permission to sell at the Bird in Hand beerhouse; Robert Dwyer at the Waterloo Hotel; Joseph Cooper at the Prospect Ina, Weston; William Treventon at the Blue Ball; and William Haywood at the Waterman's Arms, Weston Point. RcNcortis Bunter, BOARD.—Last night a ratepayers' meeting was held in the vestry of Bethesda Schoolroom for the purpose of electing a member of the Burial Board in place of the late Mr. Norman. Mr. W. Littler presided Mr. Richard Morris was proposed, seconded, and supported in eulogistic terms, and was unanimously elected to the vacant seat. BITTEN CT A WOMAN AT RllNCORN.—Margaret Water. worth, a young woman, was broueht before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, and also with assaulting Samuel Beckett, a grocer's assistant. When apprehended the priso- ner was very violent, and the officer had to call Beckett to his aid. She seized Beckett's thumb in her mouth and gave it a severe bite. She WAS ordered to pay £l. 10a 10d, or go to gaol for 21 days. BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES. The anniversary of this chapel was celebrated on Thursday evening by a tea party, at which about 100 persons were present. Subsequently a concert was held under the presidency of Mr. taeorge E. Young, of Liverpool, who in a brief speech hoped the day was not far distant when their friend Mr. Yeatman would be able to preach in a better place of worship through the liberality ef their friends in subscribing towards the cost of the erection of one. A very enjoyable entertainment of songs, pianoforte solos, and anthems by the choir, the fol- lowing taking part :—Miss Cook, Messrs. J. C. Spring, W. T. Clough, George Rashforth, E. Young, E. Carey. S. Edwatais, and Master Molyneux. KAY'S TIC PILLS, a specific in Neuralgia, Face-ache, , Is lid. Postage Id. Bold by Chemists. Kay, Brothers, Inockport.—Advt. MR. R. W. MURRAY, late managing director, and still the largest shareholder, in the Whitecross Co., is the Liberal candidate for one of the Divisions of Belfast. We need hardly say that we wish him

I every success. GUNPOWDER PLOT.—This anniversary was cele- brated in the town and district in the customary manner by the juveniles, on Thursday evening. Squibs, crackers, and other fireworks were die-. charged in every direction, and in many quarters large bonfires cast a reflection over the neighbour- hood.

MR. BRUNNER AND THE CHEMICAL TRADE.— On Tuesday evening an enthusiastic meeting in support of Mr. Brunneis candidature was held at the Drill Hall, Northwich. Mr. Shaw, president of the Runcorn Liberal Association, presided. Refer- ring to the assertion that the wages of the alkali makers at Runcorn had beenreducedin consequence of the competition of Mr.Bruniier'sworks at North- wich, he denounced it as a slanderous mis-state- ment. The truth was that the Tory manufacturers of Runcorn were screwing down their workmen's wages while the Liberal manufactqrers of Widnes found it possible to keep wages at the old level. ANOTHER GREAT CANAL benzattß.—The Berlin

correspondent of the -Daily Chronicle telegraphed on Wednesday night :—During the coming session the Government will introduce into the Reichstag a bill for the construction of the North Sea and Bal- tic Canal. The expense of construction is estimated at 1,56 million marks, or about 71 millions sterling. The execution of the work will be entrusted to Wh9 centribitte for her part the SRM of 24 millions sterling. • A DISHONEST FA SERVANT.--At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, Joseph Ashton, a farm labourer, was charged with stealing eight hampers of potatoes, value 12s 6d, the property of his master, Joseph Twiss, Laburnam Farm, Great Sankey.—The prisoner had been employed to dig potatoes, and it was ascertained that he bad sold the quantity named to another farmer. When he received the money he ran away. lie was fined 40s, or in default of pay- ment one month's imprisonment. IMPORTANT MFNINO CAS BRAINY V. RAINPORD COIL COMPA.NY, LIMITED.—This CBBB was heard before Vice-Chancellor Bristoe, at the last Liverpool sittings of the Chancery Palatine Court. ,The plain- tiff was William Brough Berry, a corn miller and farmer at Rainford, and the defendants the Rainford Coal Company, Limited. The plaintiff alleged that the water pumped by the defendants from their mines, and subsequently used by them for coal washing purposes, polluted the Rainford Brook to such an extent that the steam boilers at his mill were corroded thereby, and he was unable to use the water for domestic and agricultural purposes. The hearing lasted eight days, and a large amount of scientific and other evidence was adduced on both sides, and at the close the Vice-Chancellor reserved judgment. On Tuesday judgment was delivered at considerable length by the Vice-Chancellor, who de- cided in favour of the defendants on:Ml:the points, and dismissed the action with COSIA. THE RESPONSIBILITY OP INSIMANCE AGENTS.— At the St. Helens County Court, on Friday, the ad- journed hearing of the suit Marsh v. the Monthly Life Assurance and Endowment Co., Limited, was _

proceeded with.—The plaintiff, Levines Marsh, sued the defendant company for .£l5 insurance money due by the death of James Marsh, the father of the plaintiff. Mr. 11. L. Riley appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. M. Asti:nay represented the defendant company.—The case for the plaintiff was that the deceased, James Marsh, was induced by an agent to leave two companies—the Refuge and the British Workman—to join the defendant society, on the ex- press understanding that he would be entitled to full immediate benefit. The deceased died within

the probation period of six months, and the present action arose out of the refusal by the defendants to pay more than half benefit.—The defence was that Barnbrook, the agent, had no authority for making such a stipulation. Mr. Cottier, the secretary, was the only servant who was authorised to make such an arrangement, but he had not done so.—His Honour said if the agent promised a special benefit, he had no authority for doing so, and therefore the defendants were entitled to give only half benefit. The jury retired, and after half an hour's delibera- tion, found for the plaintiff for half the sum claimed.

JUVENILE THIEVES AT WIDNES. On Monday, at the Widnes Police Court, Joseph Quints., 11, and Robert J. Martin, 13, of Trairs and Brynn-streebs, were charged with stealing two hams, value 221 the pro- perty of Mr. John Quinn, grocer and provision dealer, Ger- rtrd-street, Simms-cross, and Catherine Quinn, mother of one of the prisoners, was charged with receiving the hams, knowing them to have been stolen. Gilbert Bolden, amist- ant to Mr. Quinn, identified the hams, which he said were worth 225. They were stolen on the 291 h ult. Police- sergeant Strickland deposed to searching the prisoners' residences, and finding the two hams produced and pieces of ethers there. The boys made statements incriminatina each other, andthe woman denied all knowledge of the theft. Martin, who has been three times previously Mort the Bench, was sentenced to fourteen days' imprisonment and four years in a reformatory; Quinn was ordered to be birched P - and Mrs. Quinn was committed ter a month's hard labour.—Thomas Dunne, 13, and Mary Dunne, 10, brother and sister, whittle parents reside at 78, 11Halwood- etreet, were charged with stealing a lady's jacket, value 20s, the property of Miss Alice Whiteside, of Rose Lea, Farn- worth, and with stealing a dolman, value ss, the property of Miss Alice Kirkham, of Halton View. Miss Whiteside said that on the 20th ult. she left the jacket produced in a room at Simms-cross Board Schools, and missed it in a couple of hours afterwards. Mr J Jameson said the jacket wee offered in pledge by the two prisoners at Mel Jameson's pawnshop, Anne-street West, on the 21st alt. The girl carricl the garment, and requested witness to lend as much as 'possible upon it. lie asked whose property it was, and the 'boy said it belonged to Mrs. Benson, of 3. Crtenfell-street. He lent Sie upon it. P.S. Macgregor deposed to apprehending the priseners, The Bench fined the girl 10s, and the 'boy was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment, afterwards to be con- fined in a reformatory for four years.

THE 3T7BILEE OF WESLEYAN METHODISM IN WIDNES. Thursday marked the completion of a very important era in the history of Weeleyan Methodiem in Widnes. Fifty 'years had elapsed since the Methodists commenced their 'labours in the town, then a pleasant riverside hamlet, and 1/ during that period of time the denemination had greatly progreesed. But a history of the society appeared in our columns about two month§ ago, and it is unnecessary to recapitulate the interesting features of its establishment and progress. The jubilee Wlll3 celebrated on Thursday biy in- teresting gatherings. In the afternoon a good congregation asesmbled in Tictoria-roadChapel, where the Rev. W. Wil- eon, chairmen of the Liverpool district, preached an elo- quent sermon on "The Jewish Jubilee." Subsequently a tea previded in the school for those who had come from various places in the circuit was partaken of by about 300 parsecs. In the evening the chapel was crowdeJ. The Rev. W. Wilson presided over the meeting, and amongst 1 those present were the Revs. R. Burdon (superintendent minister), and 3. Hothersall ; .Messrs. Abraham Leach (who preached the first Wesleyan moon in 1833, and who has now reacheci the patriarchial age of 80 years); B. Brawn, T. Robinson, C. Jones. R Fogg, T. S idler, S. Robinson, Joseph Robinson, W. Brown, P. Glover, ..Tohn Shaw. W. Duabury, and T. S. Steals. The hymns were sung to old Methodist tunes, and were heartily joined in by the large congregation. Mr, C. Taylor pre- sided at the organ. As the youngest representative present, Mr. Walter Brown, of Moss Bank Chapel, was the first speaker. Mr. John Duabury, representing Halebank, fol- lowed ; and then Mr. Joseph Williamson spoke. Mr.. Charles Jones, representing Hartland Chapel, and Mr. John Shaw, of Farnwortb, gave interesting reminiscences of Widnea Vesleyanisin. with which they had been connected about 30 yeirs. Mr. Shaw said it had been uobill work at Farnworth, where they bid great opposition, and they had

had to exercise a great deal of patience and perseverance. They did not believe is Methodism there,and the Wesleyans were called "Lone Pilgrims." The Weeleyans had no day school there, and if some of those present were in a village where they had no day schools of their own they •would find out something. There were many little influ- ences of one sort or other at work to get their children and people away from the chapel.—Mr. Themae Robinson gave an admirable addreFs explanatory of the year of jubilee.—The Chairman made an eloquent speech, on Methodist work and influence.—Mr. Abraham Leach described as the founder of Methodism in the town by the chairman, related his reminiscences in a manner which attracted the deep attention of those present. He paid a tribute to the life and and labours of Mr. William Hartland, who was unable to be present throueh illness. —Mr. Benjamin Brown mentioned many who had taken a prominent part in Wesleyan affairs, arid passed a high eulogium upon Mr. Hartland.—Addresses were delivered by Messrs. Thomas Sadler, P. Glover, Samuel Robinson, T. S. Swale, and S. B. Stringer —The collections of the day amounted to £9, and this sum will be devoted towards liquidating the debt on Moss Bank Chapel.

The monthly mesting. was held at the Town Hall, Water- loo-road, on Thursday morning. Mr. R. Shaw presided, and there were nr-sent Meesre. P. Speakman, S. Taylar, J. Meadowcrott. J. Pritchard, J. W. div.head: ourßerex OF FEVER.--IMPORTANT REPJRT.
div.p: ourßerex OF FEVER.--IMPORTANT REPJRT.

The medical officer (Dr. MacDougall) presented the fol- lowing report ;—The number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 24. Of these 7 were due to scar- let fever, 2to cancer of various organs, 2to wasting 2 to bronchitis, and one each to consumption, congestion of the brain, convulsions, apoplexy, inflammation of the lining membrane of the brain, inflammation of the wind pipe, disease of the heart, failare of the heart's action, disease of the liver, disease of the glands, and paralysis. Of the 24 deaths six were infants of one year and under, six were child- , ren one year and under five, one was over five and under ten. Of the adults two were over 20 and under 30; one was 50; one was over 50 and under 60; five were over 60 and under 70; one was 70, sad one was 80. The above 24 deaths aloe/ a death rate for the month of 18 per 1,000 of the population, a death rate which is exceptionally low for this time of the year. Scarlet fever is to be credited with seven deaths, a little over one fourth of the whole; it Is still smouldering in the eastern and north eastern districts of the town, and of all the fevers we have to contend against this is the most destructive to young life. I have reason to believe that several of the children infected con- tracted the disease at school, and, unfortunately, from the disposition of some neighbours anxious to be very neigh- bourly during the period of the greatest danger of infec- tion, viz., the peeling stage, the disease is propagated, and much mischief has been done in this way through mistaken zeal on the part of friends. Six weeks at the very least should be allowed to lapse from the first onset of an attack before an infected child is allowed to leave the home, unless an assurance is given that the peeling stage is completely over. School officials cannot exercise too mach dis- crinainatieg care in dealing with children that are sup- posed to have suffered from the fever. Before readmission, and with regard to absentees in general, schoolmasters and schoolmistresses ought to satisfy themselves , of the real cause of the child's absence from school. If the absence is due to scarlet fever or any of the other infectious fevers, it will be their duty in the in- terests of the school to take immediate steps to Prevent children from an infected house entering the school-room until they are assured that the borne is free from disease and has been thoroughly well disinfected. With regard to disinfection, I am informed that the Nuisance Inspector, who, I need hardly tell you, performs his difficult dam with becoming civility and care, has met with considerable 0p991416113 fld it would bc extremely unfortunate to have to put any legal machinery in motion in Ruh cases, but should any obstruction be offered in the future to the Nuis- ance Inspector in the diecharge of his duties, the Jaw of the

. ~., , . .. land has charged the Authority with certain obligations and invested them with certain powers, and it will be for them to say how far they will allow their authority to be disregarded with impunity, haying regard to the consetva- . _ . _

tion of the health of the township. I have during the last three months inspected several serious sanitary defects in various parts of the township that were pointed out to the Nuisance Inspector at the tithe, who has, I ant informed, reported the same to the Authority. I have recently visited these localities again and regret to say that very few if any of those necessary structural alterations have been affected. On Saturday last I inspected the greater portion of the north-eastern part of the township, more especially one locality that has been for some time a kind of nursing ground for fevers of various kinds. The ashpit arrangement is very defective and will require the immedi- ate attention of the Authority. It is not to be wondered at

if many suffer from the ill effects of decomposing organic matter when it finds it way so easily into their dwellings. It SPOMM to me that the Authority will be incurring grave responsibility if they do not Insist on these structural al- terations that were pointed out as urgently needful, to be proceeded with without much further d4.y. I feel sure the Authority is sincerely anxious that a low death rate should be maintained, a consummation which will be im- possible unless serious sanitary defects are now speedily remedied." The report concludes with a reference to a sec- tion of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, as to houses of

illfame, the Medical Officer observing that it would be abun• dantly clear to the Authority that apart from the injurious inliluenoe which the dwellers in these houses mast neces- sarily exercise in their respective localities, insanitary con• ditions were constantly met with that defied the utmost vigilance on the part of the officials to cope with them. He hoped the Board would be able to recognise the urgent necessity of co-operating with the police in dealing with these offenders, and if the Authority new fit to instruct their nuisance inspector to serve notices on persons offend- ing within the meaning of the section mentioned, it would go a long way to help to put an end t,o a grave danger to the public health. Mr. Lightbura observed that the report contained many valuable suggestions. That one with reference to school teachers was of very great importance, and immediate ac- tion should be taken. In answer to Mr. Lake, the Medical Officer said the structural arrangements at the place where the fever origi- nated were very defective. Mr. Lightburn and Mr. Dobson stated that the Health Committee had examined the places referred to in the report as having defective arrangements. Mr. Lightburn said they could not affect the alterations in a day.. .

~„ The Surveyor said on the corresponding month last year there were 34 desths, in 1833 32, and in the year previous 45. Twenty-tear seemed to be a low averaw The report was referred to the Health Coolmittee.

THE LATE MR. NORMAN. The Chairman, referring to the death of Mr. Norman, said he was Dare that it would be the plea/mere of the Board to express sympathy with the members of the family. He underetoed that Mr. Norman had been actively engaged on the Board for about 16 years, and those who had bad the pleasure of working with him bad found him alwaysdesirous of carrying out a policy for the benefit of the town. On the committees he bad been exceedingly useful and atten. tire, and that was really where a very large amount of the work of the Board was performed. The town and the Board had been deprived of a very useful member. He moved a vote of 'condolence with the family in the lees they had sus- tained. Mr. Dobson ascended the motion. By Mr. Norman's death the Board had lost a valuable member, the town a true philanthropist, and the poor a never failing friend. Mr. P. Speakman said he was a very old member of the Board himself, and he could endorse the sentiments that had been expressed with regard to Mr. Norman's work and character. Had the Board's business been his own he could not have attended to it better than he did. The motion was carried unaninionsiy. THE CHAIEMAN AND TEN LAW ,OVENN. The Chairman said the Law Clerk had admitted after Jurther consideration that he was in error in reference to the Ship Canal deputation hav- ing any interest whatever in the £l2 that was taken front the Bill; and that being the case all matters in dispute, or difference, between Mr. Linaker and himself were at an end. He had merely intimated this to the Board because he thought it was his duty to do so. VOILE IN commerres. Mr. S. Taylor was appointed chairman of the Highway and Sanitary Committee in place of the late Mr. Norman. Per- mission was granted to Mr. 11.. Beckett, contractor to the Mersev Salt and Brine Co., to make a connection with the Board's sewer at Weston Point, for the purpose of carrying off surface and ether water from the extavationawt the pro- posed dock. It was decided that a building be erected at the Town Hall in accordance with a plan prepared by the surveyor, the building to be used for storing lamps, tools, arc., the cost of erection to be defrayed out of loan account, and that tenderefor the erection be invited. It was resolved that a sub-committee be formed consisting of Messrs. Speak- man,Grice, White. and Farrell to consider the advisability of letting postingstations. The plan of Mr. It. Gibson for erection of stables and provender stied under railway arch was approved. It was decided to erect a Bray's lamp on the ground below the Market flail.—The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the past month amounted to £BBO to. Accounts amounting to £243 14 11d were passed for payment. —The Health Committee eubmitted rates for ' the rezelation of the business of the committee; and a long discussion took place upon them.
