SUCCESS OF THE SIXPENNY TELEORAIL—AIthough the Postotnce authorities are unable to furnish a tabulated statement showing in actual figures the working of the six- penny telegraph system during the few weeks it has been in operation, they have nevertheless had a sufficient experience of its working to satisfy them as to the success which has hitherto attended the cheapened rate, and the still greater success they may fairly anticipate. SENTENCE or DEaTIL—At Gloucester Assizes, on Wed- nesday, John Hill, seaman, and John Williams, painter. were sentenced to death for the murder of Ann Dickson, at Woebley, Herefordshire, on the night of September 13. The prisoners left a public-house with the deceased and another woman. The latter was grossly assaulted by Williams, and the following day the body of Dickson, with her face and skull beaten in, was found in a field. The judge held out I no hope of mercy.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT RUNCORN.

Runcorn Public Hall was svell filled on Monday evening by an assembly gathered in support of Mr. W..H..Verdin. the Conservative candidate for the Northwich Division. Ad- mission was by ticket, but there were many Liberals pre- sent. The proceedings were of a quiet and orderly character. Mr. C. Wigg, president or the Conservative Association, I occupied the chair, and on the platform were the Right Hon. Lord Harris (Under Secretary of State for India), the Revs. W. Preston, E. 0. Rawson (vicar of Marston), T. Mad- den, R. Edwards, J. Lockwood (vicar of Halton), Mr. W. H. Verdin (Ike candidate), Captain Hazlehurst, J.P., Cap- tain Jolliffe, Dr. Steele, Messrs. W. Hayes, J. Brundrit, J.P., A. Thomas, J.P., G. L. Wigg, H. Cooke, It. A. Zer- burg (Conservative candidate for Chester), Joseph Verdin, A. N. Hornby (Nantwich), W. Lord (Widnes). E. Tim- mins, A. Buck, J. H. Salkeld, F. A. Lake, W. H. Roger- son, F. Ockleston, J. H. S ,Ikeld, E. Nlstwood, T. F. Ac- ton, J. J. Speakman, P. Smith, .1. W. Lightburn, C. Hughes, G. Connor, W. J. Shore. J. H. Holland, rie. The Chairman, who was received wiih cheers and some hissing, remarked that he wan tic, great p,litician. His time had been too much taken up in husioess matters to devote much of it to politics, and he ti not profess ro be an ora- tor; but he thought in a crisis like this it behoved every Englishman to exert himself. (Applause) Mr. Verdin, who WAP greeted with cheers and groans, alluded to the fact that h- was A ratepayer in the town, and offered his sytnpethv to the working men on the depression in the chemical and every other trade. It was not only the works tkat were unprofitaule but ships were tied up in almost every port in the couutry, %shier' showed that tEct trade generally was in a most unp-ofitable and unhealthy condition; but the Commisnioo would be able to ascer amu tne reason why our ships were tied up, and he might mer.- tion as one of the reasons that other countries were offering bounties that encourage German and French ships, and thus prohibit our ships taking our manufactures into those countries where we used to send them. (Applause) After alluding to the importance of the colenies for the porpose„ ef trade, Mr. Verdin spoke of free education. He thought they would find that free education meant that the Blhle would be abolished from our schools. because Mr. Chamber- lain—(cheers)—had said that the only consequence would be that religion would cease. If that was the case, tbs I Bible would be abolished from our schools. (Loud cries of "No," and "Never.") Mr. W. Hayes moved a resolution to support Mr. Verdin, who he recommended those present to vote for becauee he was a member of the salt trade, which Mr Brunner was trying to ruin. (Applause.) He had nothing whatever to say against Mr. Brunner. He had made lots of money, and he made very good use of it. He hoped he would continue to do so, " but he was not the man for Galway." (Laughter and applause.) Mr. J. Kilcross seconded the motion, which was put to the meeting amid cheers and counter cheers, and a large show cd hands against it. The Chairman declared the resolution carried. Mr. Verdin then answered a large number of questions which had been handed up. The first was—lf elected, will you support the policy of Lord Salisbury or Lord Randolph Churchill ? (Cheers and groans.)—As a rule, there is but one captain on board each vessel, and the captain's orders are followed.

Have you any remedy that you could propose for the de- pression in trade, and if so, what? Yes. Keep the Conser- vative Government in office. (Loud cheers and groans.) The presence of a registrar is necessary at a marriage in a Nonconformist Church, will you vote for a measure to abolish this anomalous, harassing, and expensive custom ? I have already answered that question at Northwich in the affirmative. (Applause.) Church clergymen in the possession of rich livings often appoint curates at a miserably low stipend to perform the services of the Church, and never, or seldom, assume the sacerdotal functions themselves. Are you in favour of remedying this edmitiedirr wiCted practice, and if so, by what means ?—There are one or two statemente which I Cannot altogether agree with, but the curate's salary might be remedied in this way; by the congregation sub!cribing little more freely. (Applause and hooting.) . Are you in favour of the Disestablishment of the Church of England if unaccompanied by dieendowment ?—I am not Is favour of the Disestablishment or disendowment of the English Church. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) Will a proposal to revise the incidence of taxation receive your support ?—Yee. In the Runcorn and other Unions the tenants of property, farming and otherwise, have to pay a sanitary rate which is expended in carrying out schemes permanently improving a landlord's property and land. Would you vote for a measure compelling the landlord tr pay his fair share ? Whatever is the landlord's fair share I shall be very happy to request him to pay. (Cheers.) As the house and park of an entailed estate cannot be seized for debt, would you vote for an Act to extend the same privilege to the labourer's cottage ?—lit order to en- tail an estate it takes some little money, and if the labourer entails his cottage a good portion of the value of the cottage to a great extent would be gone in law ex- penses. • As the ratepayers of Runcorn had to pay their quota to- wards the freeing of the Dee Bridges, would you vote for the freeing of Runcorn footbridge-,(clieers and laughter)— which is essentially a county bridge, by the county rates? (Loud cheers.)—That is a matter which I should have to ' consider seriously, but I may tell you that as regards the , Chester bridge my brother was the only magistrate who op • paged the grant of the money. (Cheers). You object to Sunday labour at Winnington. What is ' the difference between Sunday labour at Winnington and Sunday labour at Wigg Brothers and Steele? (Cheers and laughter.) —The difference is this. The work that is done by Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steel is necessary. Most of tbe work which is done at Winnington is unnecessary. (Cheers and laughter). Yon have publicly stated that Messrs. Brunner, Mond and Co. have been the cause of the depression in the chem- ical trade in the district through the eetablishment of works at Winnington. What action would you have taken if the patent by which Brunner. Mood and Co. carry on their w.rks had been in your possession ? (A Voice: "Don't answer.")—Gentlemen, that is a hypothetical ques- tion. I am afraid I cannot answer that. If another German prince were to come and join our Royal German band—(loud laughter)—would you vote for bids a large salary? (Laughter and cheers.) I ani siad to hear the people of Runcorn are so musical, and that you have a German band. (Laughter.) But it is a ques- tion for the ratepayers to consider, about grarting a large salary. (Applause, and a voice: "Answer the question.) The Liberals of Runcorn have been charged by your followers with packing their recent meeting by the issue of tickets, What is your opinion of the present assembly ? (Laughter.) I have a very faveurable opinion of the pre- sent &numbly. (Cheers and groans.) Are your in favour of imposing a duty upon foreign manufactured articles imported into this country? Have you any objection to an import duty being imposed in Ire- land upon English goods? This gentleman wishes ma to settle the affairs of the nation in five minutes. (Laughter.) I caunot possibly undertake to do that. Will yon vote for the Deceased Wife's Sisters Bill ? (Laughter.) I will do with that so. (Throws it on one aide.) Will a proposal to tax hicycies and tricycles receive your vote. (Laughter.) No. As you confidently anticjpate shortly being in London as tile elected representative_of this constituency, will you vote for the removal of liquor licencee from private clubs P (Laughter.) I believe they have no licences, but I think they ought to have a lioence as well as the public-houses. (Cheers.) Are you of Lord Harris's opinion that Croseland's bowl- ing is unfair ? (Roars of laughter.) Mr. Verdi' did not reply to the question. What is your candid opinion of the song, "Brunner and victory ?" (Prolonged laughter and cheers.) My candid "opinion is that the song is very much like the candidate, a very poor one. (Laughter' and cheers.) Lord Harris, who was loudly cheered, said that if the gentleman who put the questiou with regard to Crossland's bowling would come on the platform he would probably find that his lriend, Mr.. Hornby, and himself, held different opinions, and between the two he might have some little difficulty in coming to an agreement on that point. (Applause and laughter.) Referring to Irish affairs, his Lordship said that there were two kinds of Home Rule. There was the more serious and larger question of an Imperial Parliament in Dublin, which should have power to deal with questions of Imperial interest—the questions of army and navy, the ex- ports and imports of trade in Ireland. These were questions which, in the interests of Great Britain, it was necessary should be maintained in the Imperial Parliament. It was impossible to consider for one moment the disintegration of the empire. (Cheers.) There was the smaller question of Home Rule, very similar to that which had been raised in England—local self-government. He viewed with the deepest regret and shame the illtreatment that, be thought. Ireland had received from England in the past, and he hoped it would be the object of succeeding Parliaments, succeeding Ministers, whether Tory or Liberal, to endeavour to mete out to Ireland a fairer system of treatment (Hear, hear, and cheers.) Whichever party was in power after the election—the Tory or the Radical—it would be impossible to leave Ireland untouched by a measure of local self-government. He declared that should anything happen to Mr. Gladstone Mr. Chamber- lain would assume the leadership of the Radical and Liberal party, and the disestablishment of the English Church would at once become a question of practical politics. (Ap- planse.) Disestablishinent meant very little, but disendew- ment meant a great deal, and he did not think it possible to effect disestablishment without accompanying it with diet- endowment. Be believed the cry for disestablishment and disendowment was not a recognised one throughout the country. The Tories were willing to take up the question of small holdings in a legal and natural way. They ac- knowledged the difficulty of passing land from band to band, hut that was a question in which they were in the hands of the lawyers. (Applause.) Speeches were delivered by Mr. R. A. Yerburgh and the Rev. E. 0. Rawson.

Mr. Verdin was then asked if he would vote for Home Rule, and replied that he was in favour of giving full and equal justice to Ireland, but opposed to the disintegration of the empire. • vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the pro- ceedings.
And
ELECTION SONG--

MARCH, BOYS, MARCH. Air: Tramp, tramp. 0 ye lovers of the right, Get ye ready for the fight, And away with him who dare not face the storm; Think upon your sires of old, And be resolute and bold, While you strike a blow for Freedom and Reform.. Cuontrs. March, boys, march to meet the Tories; Verdin is nowhere in the fray. There's a champion in the field, And he does not mean to yield— J. T. Brunner is the man to win the day. Now we've got the vote at last, Let us not forget the past; We must tell the Tories that they plead in vain• . Since the vote came from the Rads, On the polling day, my lads, We must let the Liberals have it back again. March, boys, 'march, &c. There's a Verdin on the scene, , And they call him Verdant Green; He wouldlike to be M.P., but he will fail. We have Brunner bright and clear— He's the bird we like to hear, For you can't put any " salt " upon his tail. March, boys, march, &c. We must send to Parliament One who'll truly represent Every section with a feeling for his kind; One who wants to see fair play, And who doesn't block the way— lie must be a man of merit and of mind. March, boys, march, &c. We have got a righteous cause; What we want is equal laws, the "Grand Old Man" put in his proper place; We are gaining strength each hour, While the foe is losing power— We are fighting for the freedom of the race. . March, boys, march, &c. —ED., .Ex.

Those who have studied his career know that this is the simple truth; but to the law and to the testimcrny 1. .Who (backed up by all the local Orangemen) •caused the retirement of Mr. Ireland-Black- burne from the representation of Warrington because he had the courage to vote in favour of the Maynooth Grant? •Sir GILBERT GREENALL. 0. Sir GILBERT GREENALL. la Who voted against Mr. Meldon's Irish Fran- chise Bill? Sir GILBERT GREENALL. 14. Who has not a single word about Ireland in his - present address to the electprs ? Sir GILBERT GREENATA. Inrsinrxx,—Be not deceived. Sir Gilbert Greenall has neither changed nor repented. lie has no re- gret for his acts of hatred in the past; lie makes no promise of amendment in the future. If we vote for kim, we shall, vote against ourselves ; we shall be traitors t 6 our country, and traitors to our re- ligion.

• • SIR GiL BET GREENALL AND THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME. "An Elector" has published the following ex- posure on this subject:— The Tories are very anxious to persuade the Electors of Warrington that their Candidate has been. a friend of this great scheme, but, as the following facts will show, Sir Gilbert Greenall had positively done nothing to promote the Manchester Ship _ Canal undertaking until the present election car,l paign had commenced. If this great work found no better friends that he has been, the, ship Canal Bill would never have been obtained. QUESTION, ANSWER. When the first Warring- ton Committee was be- Sir Gilbert creenaii j. ing formed, Sir Gilbert fused to, allow his Greenall was asked to name be connected allow his name to be with the Warrington. placed on such Corn- Cu:ntmittee of the Ship mittee. °anal. What was hl6 reply ?
How much did Sir Gil- bert Greensll subscribe towards the enormous expense incurred by the promoters of the Ship Canal in their First Application to Parliament P
Not a Single Penny.
How much did he sub- , scribe towards the cost of the Second Applica- Not a Farthing-. tion to Parliament?
flow much did he sub- scribe towards the ex- pense of the Third Application to Parlia- ment ?
Nothing..

Sir Gilbert Greenall has therefore not given a fraction towards the costs of obtaining the Ship Canal Bill, which have amounted altogether to the sum of One Hundred Thousand Pounds. When the Ratepayers of Warrington voted so unanimously in favour of levying a Rate of Twopence in the Pound His voting paper was re- towards the expense of turned Unfilled up. promoting the Ship Canal Bill, What did Sir Gilbert Greenall do? For the construction of the Canal, a large portion of the Walton Estate will be required, and for this land the promoters will have to pay Sir Gilbert Greenall the full market value, and ten per cent, in addition for compulsory sale, so that beyond receiv- ing the full price for his land he will be entitled to thousands of pounds besides. In return for all this, what has he done for the Ship Canal now? Although the Prospectus of the Ship Canal had. been before the public for weeks, Sir Gilbert Green- all never subscribed for a single share, until Messrs. Rothschild, the great financiers, had guaranteed to the promoters of the Ship Canal to raise what capital was necessary to carry out the scheme. So that from first to last Sir Gilbert Greenall has not placed a single penny in this great scheme until all risk of loss had vanished, and he was absolutely assured of making a large snm of money out of the undertaking. Working-men, compare for yourselves the paltry amount which Sir Gilbert Greenall has invested in the Ship Canal on the one hand, -with the vast benefits which the scheme will bestow upon him on the other, and show by your votes that yon are neither to be hoodwinked nor humbugged by the Tory Candidate.

dough., , Mrscsa.r.aszons —The following were dealt with for drunkenness :—Timothy Senealy, in Buttermarket-street, on Saturday, ordered to pay costs; Philip McGuire, in Horseruarkkt.street, on Saturday, -fined 5s and costs; Ann Ford, in Winwick-street, on Sunday morning, sent to prison for 14 days; John Peers, in Winwick-street, on Sunday, fined 58 and costs; Binnery Hines, in Hill•street, on the 25th ult., fined 5s and costs.—Edward Griffin, for being drunk and disorderly in Lyme-street, on Saturday evening, and assaulting a person named John Casten, in Bridge- street, was rent to prison for a month, and ordered to be bound over to keep the peace.—Rabert Burns, for being drunk and disorderly in Ship-yard, on Saturday night, and breaking a window of the house of his father, was sent to prison for two months.—James Ryder was fined 2a fid, in- cluding costs, for allowing a greater number of persons to lodge in his house than it was registered for.—Gee. WADDINGTON V. ROCHDALE 11011b1HT9,—This match took place at Rochdale on Saturday last, Warrington being minus Turner, Dillon, Jolley, and Barnes, whose places were taken by Ashby, Hough, Nevins, and Littlewood. The ground was in a wretched condition, owing to the heavy rains, and the Warrington men did Lot seem partial to the ground at all, while their opponents were quite at home in the mud. Warren kicked off, Smith returning to half way. From the scrimmage Smith again got pos--ession, and put in a good kick, the ball going over the line ; Ashby touched down. Settle good kicks were put in by Griffiths, Bamford, and Gil-, lout, the play being taken to half way, where Gilbert and 4cleakman showed some good dribbling to touch line. Here * home forwards broke away, and Warrington were again -*impelled to save. From the kick off the ball was returned •-ly,Griffirhs, Ashby again saving. On the ball being brought out, Gilbert followed well up, and carried the ball to the • home 25, but Smith got possession, and making a Wee run, kicked the ball over the line, the ball going dead. Some tight scrimmages now took place, and friillicivn getting hold, passed forward to Rhodes, who obtained a try. The War- rington captain appealed. but it was ruled against him. From the kick off -.Nevins followed well up, and aided by Gilbert and Povey, carried the ball to the home 25. From the scrimmage the home forwards broke away, but Warren saved, and the visitors, after a lot of scrimmages, forced the ball over the line, a touch-down resulting. •On bringing the ball out, Taylor got the ball from Nolan by another forward pass, and running, well grounded the ball over the line. Warren appealed again, but with no use. On F. Turner kicking off, Wilde returned, and following up quick, obtained the third try for Rochdale, from which Taylor kicked a goal. After this the visitors played up well and gradually worked the ball to home quarters' where Warren made a good pass to Hough, but this player failed to see his chance, and instead of running, kicked, the ball going into touch-in-goal, when half-time was called. On re- suming the Rochdale captain kicked off, the ball being well returned by Massey. A scrimmage took place and Smith getting hold made a short run, but was collared by Massey. From the scrimmage Warren made a good run, and passed to Massey, who kicked, the ball going into touch at the home 25. From the, line out Smith again got pos- session, hut was well brought down by Ashton. From the scrimmage the ball Has passed to Bamford, who got in a long kick, Ashby touching down. On kicking out Davies put in a good dribble to half-way, where a scrimmage was formed. Gilbert getting away kicked down the field, Buck- ley returning well. From the scrimmage Warren passed to Massey, who rounded his men in good style, and wouid have certainly crossed the line if he had not hesitated and thrown the chance away. From the line out the Warrington forwards took the ball over the line, a dead ball result- ing. On kicking off some good kicks were put in by the backs, the ball finally being touched down by Ashby. From this time nothing tok place of any importance, the score standing Rochdale, one goal, two tries, and five minors ; to Warrington three minors. For Warrington the forwards played a sterling game, Warren and Gilbert playing in their usual form. Warrington : Ashby, full back: Buxton, Massey, and Hough, three-quarter backs; Warren (captain) and Gilbert, ball-hacks; Ashton, Turner, Davies, Speakman, Heyes, Povey, Nevins, Savage, and Littlewood, forwards; umpire Mr. T. Barnes. Rochdale : Buckley, full hick; Smith;Bamfoid, and Taylor, three-quarter backs; Griffiths and Nolan. half-backs; Wilde, Wilson, Grove, Rhodes, Milliden, Slater, Rankin, Brierley, and Bares, forwards. Referee, Mr. Hunter. We may say that the visitors were misled about the referee. Mr. Roger Walker, of Manchester, Was down for this position, and not until after the match did the Warrington men know that another man had taken his place.

ASSOCIATION RULES. LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT CHALLENGE CUP. Saturday last being the day for the completion of the first round of th:. competition for the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup the following local ties were played : WAIIRINGToN V. SANKEY REFINERS. This tie was played at Warrington on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the home team by three go&ls to two. The ball WaS kicked off at 3-20, Warrington playing against the wind. Sankey scored from the foot 1 T;ole after two minutes' play, and Murray put one through immediately after. War- rington now got well together and raced well up the field. Dodging Corcoran, Clarke put in a low fast sbDt, which proved too much for Theme. Warbur ton was applauded for a smart piece of play, and he put the ball well in goal. Thane fisted out, and Shaw was finely tackled by Day. Cooke passed to Clarke at right wiug, who sent in a good, shot, Thane appearing to be under the bar wh.n banding out. Clarke again g the hall, aad centred alcely to Shaw, who heat Thane with a fast shot. The game was now level,

and both sides worked hard. Corcoran gave some tremen- dous kicks but they were quietly sent back by Hind and I Dowd. Roberts got possession, and staving off the forwards I got a good shot in, abicb the centres tried to improve, Thane holding the ball shortly after was charged, and fell i I heavily on his shoulder, necessitating a stoppage of the game. He retired and took no further part in the game, t Day and Corcoran played up well, bat could not keep eat the home forwards. crossing' over with the score equal, I Warrington seen assumed the aggressive, and se close was I the game kept that the home goal was but once neared. Sankey were kept back, and several corners were conceded. Clarke succeeded in eluaing Corcoran and again scored, while shortly after a shot from along the goal line struck the posts. O'Hara and Corcoran played a sterling game be- hind, while Hughes and Thane on the right played well to- I gather. The Warrington half-backs, Roberts and Warbur- ton, were cool and certain, and to their play a great deal of the credit is due. Teams :—Sankey Refiners: Thane, goal; O'Hara and Corcoran, backs ; Callaghan and Day, half-backs ; Percival, Murray, Unsworth, Toole, Thane, Hughes, forwards. Warrington : Hamilton, goal; Hind and Dowd, backs ; Warburton and Roberts, balf-backs ; Clarke, Critchlev, Shaw, Cooke, Parker, and Gill, forwards. Beferee, Mr. J. Cameron. STANLEY V. HAYDOCK Sr. JAMES —These clubs met at Walton-stiles, Liverpool, on Saturday, to play their tie. Rain was falling when the teams faced each other, and it was decided to play two 30's. Anderson and Pimblett, for Haydock, played a capital game, and ware mainly respon- sible for keeping down the home team's score. No point was scored at half-time. On changing ends Stanley con- tinued pressing their opponents, Kerr troubling Williams to fist out a lofty shot. Anders "n made things look better for Haydock by a nice bit of passing, and B. Williams gave , Wright a chance of handling the ball for once. As no goal had been scored when time was called, half-au-hour's extra play was decided upon, the feature of which was a grand run by W. Wilson down his wing, ending by mewing I acroes to Grant, who sent in a shot which beat the Havdock I custodian. No further point was scored in the game, which thus ended in favour of Stanley by one goal to nil. Teams :—Stanley : G. Wright, goal; R. Stevenson and G. Dove)+, backs; G. Kerr, J. Phillips, and R. M'Callum, half backs: W. Brown and W. Wilson, left wing ; J. Culkin, centre; J. Wilson and J. Grant, right wing. Haydock St. James T. Williams, goal ; H. Anderson and T. Pim- blett, backs; T. Rimmer, J. Spencer, and J. King, half backs; J. Chisenhale and B. Williams, left wing; A. Ander- , ton, centre; W. Williams and J. Wilson, right wing. EARLESTOWN WANDERERS V. TRANMERE.—This tie was played at Earlestown on Saturday. There was a good at- I tendance of spectators, considering the unpropitious weather. I Tranmere won the toss, and played with the wind. Tran- I mere scored the only goal in the first half, but the referee disallowed it. The second portion of the game was entirely in favour of the Wanderers, who scored four goals (one not allowed) to their opponents' nil, the last three being put through in five minutes, the home team thus winning by three goals to none. Champion, J. Shaw, and Thompson (Earlestown), and Coppack, T. Myers, and Allerton (Tran- • mere) played a good game. Traumere, we understand, laid , a protest against the Wanderers' ground being unfit to play . on. Teams :—Earleetown Wanderers: T. Champion, goal; W. Lord and H. Selby, backs; W. Allison, J. Lowe, and R. Johnson, half baeks ; J. Holt and A. Allan, right wing ; T. Thompson, centre; J. Shaw and W. Shaw, left wing. Tran- mere : G. Coppack, goal; J. Miller and W. Walters, backs; A. Lobb, R. Benyon, and J. Myers, halfbacks; J. Hargrave. and T. Myers, right wing; J. liesketh, centre; T. White- head and W. Allerson, left wing. HAYDOCK (LATE TEMPERANCE) V. LIVERPOOL Sr. BENE- DicTs.—These teams met on the Wagon Inn ground, Hay- dock, to decide their tie. There was a fair attendance of spectators. The visitors winning the toss took advantage of the wind. The game was well contested during the first "45," and both sides scored two goals. On the change of ends, Haydock pressed the visitors severely, and scoring four goals to the Saints none entered the second round by six goals to two. Teams : Taylor, goal; Baines and Hatton, backs ; King and Allen, half backs; Blackey (captain), Moran, Wedgwood, Arnold, Harrison. and Twist, forwards. St. Benedict's: Jones, goal; T. Whittle and Bolton, backs; Patterson, Dykes, and Jones, half backs; J. Whittle (captain), Briscoe, Gilder, Pool, and Rabey, for- wards. Dneav FOR SECOND Romen.—A meeting of the com- mittee of the Liverpool and District Football Association was held at the Neptune Hotel, Liverpool, on Monday even- ing, when Mr. A. B. Hall (president), occupied the chair. The principal business was to consider the protest of the Earlestown F. C. (cupholders) who had been thrown out of the first round of the competition by the Bromborough Pool F. C. The Earlestoeians protested against R. Roberts, who played for their epponents, on the ground that he was not a recognised member of the club, and that he resided out- side the limits of the association. The committee upheld the protest, and ordered the tie to be replayed at Brom- borough next Saturday week. The draw for the second round then took place with the following result :—New Ferry v. Everton, Bootle Christ Church v. St. Peter's, nal- mersdale v. Whiston, Warrington v. Linacre, Newsome v. Iclaydock. G-olborne v. Stanley, Southport Christ Church v. Earlestown Wanderers, Southport High Park v. Toxteth Wanderers, Earlestown or Bromborough v. Cambrian, Southport v. Bootle.

Bradford last week had a tour to Scotland to oppose the crack Rugby clubs. The first match was against the West of Scotland, out of which they came with flying colours, the Tykes having won by one goal, one try, and four minors, to three minors. On Monday they tackled the Edinburgh Acidemicals, but contrary to expectation, the Academicals won by one try. This is the first defeat of the Yorkshire men this season. OR the Tuesday they met Edinburgh University, the result being a draw; Bradford, one minor, University three minors. Bradford in this match played without flawcridge and Ritchie. Swinton received a visit from the Yorkshire cuoholdere, and those who had assembled witnessed a grand game, though the ground, owing to the late rains, was against brilliant runs. Eventually the game ended in a draw, Batley six minors to Swinton two minors. A fine game was witnessed between Manchester and Broughton on the Whalley Range grounds, the result being a draw ; Broughton one try and six minors, to one try and four minors. The county teams are getting into harnees, Yorkshire already having had two trial matches. North Lancashire will oppose South Lancashire at Barrow to-day. The Neal) should win easily as the seam is considerably stronger than the South. On Monday last the new rules for the guidance of umpires and referees came into force. Broughton .Rangers proved too strong for Oldham, al- though neither team was fully represented. At call of time the result was Rangers four tries and one minor to nil. A capitally-contested yams was that played on the Sal- ford ground between that club and hull. The visitors had a good reputation, but in this .ease they had to submit to defeat, as Salford won after a very hard game by two tries and six minors to four minor*. The elements prevented most of the Liverpool clubs from turning out. Widnes jaunted over to Wigan to try conclusions with that club, a well-contested game ending in a draw. Widnee one try and tour minors to Wigan one try and three minors. Warrington took a very poor team to oppose Rochdale fißornete, being minus Barnes, Jolley, and Turner, and, as could only have been expected, they were defeated by one goal, two tries, and six minors to a couple of minors, but I presume the way in which they were entertained afterwards will help to heal the wound. Runcorn should have played Bootle, but that club failed to turn up, causing the Runcorn club a serious lose. If the executive of the West Lancashire acid Border Towns Rugby Union were invested with the power of expelling such clubs from the union, such causes of complaint would ceaee. St. Helene Recreation opposed Wavertree at Liverpool, a good game ending in a draw. Recreation four minors to a brace of minors.

DEATH OF THE RENt. J. P. MBESELL—The death of .the Rev. S. P. Mursell, the well•known Baptist minister, who, together with the late Mr. Ed. Miall, founded the Libera- tion Society, died at Leicester on Monday night. The de- ceased succeeded the Rev. Robert Hall, and the Rev. Arthur Muesli, the popular preacher, is his son. He was over 80 years of age: MR. BRIGHT AT B/RMINGRAM.—Mr. John Bright began his canvass for the central division of Birmingham by ad- dressing a crowded meeting on Thursday night in the Town Hall. He reviewed the history of the past fifty years to show that the iorq party had opposed soecessive measures of useful reform and had in each case to surrender to the popular will. Their blind and obstinate resistance had been followed by humiliating capitulations. He strongly con- demned the proposed expedition into the territories of King Thebaw, and denounced a warlike policy generally, saying he hoped that the time was coming when no Government would be tolerated that declared war except from absolute necessity and in a just cause.

Great floods have prevailed in the Lower Treat Valley. The reads have been submerged, and boatmen have been busily engaged. Farm property is much damaged. At Exeter Assizes on Monday, John Oke Harris, share- broker, was sentenced to five years' penal sarvitude for 'frauds on a building society of which ho was manager. On Saturday morning, David Thomas, cattle dealer, of Cowbridge, Glamorganshire, WAS found a few yards from his own door, lying dead with a large wound in his head..

A destructive fire broke out on Monday morning in a warehouse belonging to Messrs. S. Spriggs and Co., in the Back-gorse, Liverpool, which was stored with loose cotton, , ship chandlery, and other produce. On Monday morning between 2,000 and 3,000 weavers came out on strike from the cotton spinning mills in the east end of Glasgow. as a protest against a proposed re- duction in the rate of piece work to the extent of 7i per cent.

Mr. Frank Stock, accountant, went to a mill in Ashton- under-Lyne, on Monday morning, to induce voters working there to go and poll for one of the municipal candidates, and was killed by a hoist while going from one part of the build- ing to another. A fire occurred on Monday, in some out-buildings at Bed- stead, surrey, in which from 20 to 30 potato pickers were sleeping. An old man named Clifford was burnt to a cin- Ider, and two women were seriously injured. The fire was caused loy the falling of a lighted candle. -. , .

PROPOSED MEMORIAL STATTAI TO BISHOP FRASER.—At a public meeting, attended by prominent Dissenter, as well as Churchmen, in Manchester, on Monday, it was resolved to erect a suitable memorial statue to Dr. Fraser in some con- spicuous position in the city, and that any surplus funds be applied as determined at a future meeting. Letters of apology for non-attendance had been received from the 'Bishop of Chester, Lord Wintuarleigh, Lord Derby, and llothers. Lord Derby wrote from Knowsley :—" I regret that engagement, here will put it out of my power to attend the meeting to be held tomorrow for the purpose of consi- dering how best to do honour to the memory of the late Bishop, whose public spirit, devotion to duty, and genuine liberality of mind have well earned such a mark of respect from the people of Manchester." Mr. Hugh Mason, M.P., wrote :—•• I shall feel pleasure in givinE a subscription for the purpose of the memorial, and beg to enclose £5O. There never lived a man who was more henoured and esteented by Christians of every section than Dr. *reser. We Die. senters deeply mourn for his loss." The Roman Catholic Bishop of Salford wrote I shall be happy to take part in any suit 4ble memorial of a purely civil or philan- thropic character, such, for instance, as an addition to our hospitil accommodation." After the meeting bad separated letters were received from the following :—The Earl of Docie (enclosing a cheque for £10), Mr. H. W. FATAL FIRM AT SOUTHPORT.—A fire broke out on Mon- day morning at No. 26, Seabank-road, Southport, in the occupation of Mrs Sarah Elizabeth Hutchinson, aged about 50. Two men entered the house by the front bedroom win- dow. They found the bed on fire, and en it lay the dead body of Mrs Hutchinson, fully dressed. The bed and its contents were burned to ashes. It is supposed to have been ignited by a reading limp. HEROISM RECOONISED.—The heroic deed of Thos. White, the coastguardsman, who was the means of saving the lives of six children at Ryhope, near Sunderland, a few weeks ago, will still be fresh in the public memory. He has been the recipient of a neat and elegant gold medal !rem the children of the Jesmond Wesleyan Church Sunday School as a mark of the high respect and esteem in which his noble action is held by the children and teachers. . WEST LANCASHIRE RAILWAY COMPANY.—The report of the direotors shows that the total income of the company for the half-year amounts to £9,016, as compared with (19,200 in the corresponding period of last year, being an in- crease Of £715, £527 of which is due to increased passen- ger traffic. The Board were happy to state that the con- struction of the Liverpool; Southport, and Preston Junction I Railway *as being pushed forward vigorously. MOTT/W.—At Leicester and Derby Assizes, on Monday, 28 colliers were charged-with taking part in a riot and wrecking houses. Nineteen pleaded guilty, and nine not guilty. , No evidence having been adduced, the nine were ' discharged. Those who pleaded gnilty expressed their regret lat their conduct, and the bench, taking into consideration the fact that they had resumed work and had already under- gone 14 days' Confinement, bound them over to appear when called Upon. The Tory party were trying, in two ways, to impair the Liberal success, which they were afraid would follow the great change which had taken place in the county suffrage. They were trying to avoid the particular issue before the country by confusing the minds of the people with criti- cisms on the foreign policy of the late Government. ,The members of the late Government had admitted, on looking back at what had occurred, that while they had done their best, yet some of the matters with which they • had to deal were so complicated that they made some mistakes.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING IN THE NORTH.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING IN THE NORTH.
EAST WARD:

On Thursday evening a meeting of the' electors of North-East Ward was held in• Brick-street School- room, in support of the Liberal candidate, Mr. W. Crosfield, J.P. Thirty minutes before the time ad- vertised for commencing the proceedings, the room was crowded, and when the candidate, accom- panied by several friends, entered the room, he I received a most flattering greeting. Mr. Howes, who was also present, and spoke vigorously for over an hour, was thoroughly in touch with the meeting, and his remarks were constantly interrupted by rounds of applause. After the meeting, so much favour did he find with the audience, that they as- sembled outside the building and gave hearty cheers for Mr. Howes and other gentlemen who had taken part in the proceedings. Mr. Z. Armitage occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Mr. W. Crosfield, J.P., Mr. Howes, Mr. John Platt, J.P., Dr. Gornall, J.P., Mr. A. Browne, and Mr. IL Roberts.

The CHAIRMAN said that it was only a fortnight since the .contest began,. and now they were in the thick of it; every- one bad warmed to the work. He deprecated the use of personalities, but, of ; course, he said, they were obliged to criticise the speeches of their opponents, and were quite at liberty, to do so. At the same time they had a far more important work to do, and he urged them to put forth every effort ha furtherance of the Liberal canke.• (Ap- plause.) • Mr.' WILLIAM CROSFIELD, who. was cheered on rising, said that a great deal was being said nowadays about free trade and fair trade, and it was difficult to get at an author- itative statement with regard to the claims of fair trade, and the attacks made upon free trade. There were many voices, but no great number of them spoke with authority. But speaking now they had the advantage of a very authori- tative and emphatic speech delivered the previous evening by Lord Salist,ury on the subject of trade. Lord Salisbury told his audience that lie and his friends were anxious to in- 1 quire into the present depression in many branches of trade, and had decided to establish a Commission to inquire into it. He also said that the Liberals did all in their power to make that inquiry an impossibility. This was a charge that had often been hrought against the free traders—a numerous body. The fact was that a large number of fair traders, of Tories, and of men who were known to be unfavourable to free trade were formed into a commission, and one by one a few Liberals and a few earnest free traders were asked to take a seat upon the comm'ssion. They never showed any, disposition to have a fair representation of those who believed in the existing principles of trade, and hence the unwillingness of earnest Liberals to waste their time on such an inquiry. Mr. Goschen, one of those invited, said—" I refuse to serve on the Royal Commission because I do not believe it would be any good whatever." Lord Salisbury said that some people alleged that the Conservatives were enemies to free trade and were in favour of a dear loaf by the re-imposition of the corn laws. Lord Salisbury said—" I need not tell von that, to Rae Lord Iddealeigh's classical language, it is a down-right thumping lie." Mr. Bartlett. speaking at the Public Hall a fortnight ago' distinctly said that we could not expect prosperity and happiness throughout the land, more particularly in the agricultural districts, with corn at 30s. That meant,if anything at all, that they must have corn at a higher price, and that meant a dearer loaf. (Hear, hear.) He would leave Lord Salisbury and Mr. Ashmead Bartlett to settle that question between them, as to which of them was indulging in the expression that Lord Salisbury used. Lord Salisbury said that the Conservatives pointed the working-man forward to obtain wealth that was yet un created. (Laughter.) The Liberals bad rather congre tulate people on the wealth that had been created--(ap- plause)—which was already in their pockets, the wealth ; the possession of which was the natural result of free trade. Lord Salisbury said that wealth could not be gained with- out capital. lie (Mr.. Crosfield) would appeal to the &a- -1 perience of his audience. He had no doubt that they knew many men in Warrington who were to-day wealthy, who , began with nothing but their own brains and the strength of their muscles and sinews. If Lord Salisbury would in- quire he would find' that the wealth of Lancashire and the backbone of England had resulted not from capital, but from labour. (Applause.) Mr. Crosfield proceeded to fur- ther criticise the remarks of Lord Salisbury, and was fre- quently applauded. Mr. J. BRostear proposed "That this meeting of the north-east electors pledges itself to use every legitimate effort to secure the triumphant return of William'Crostield, 'Esq., J.P., at the forthcoming Parliamentary election by a large majority." He referred to trade depression in able terms. Mr. JOHN PLATT seconded the resolution, and asked his audience to do their utmost, one and all, to return Mr. Crosfield. , The resolution was carried and duly acknowledged by Mr' 11 Crosfield. Mr. Howes then addressed the meeting. Be referred at length to the Trade Commission arid criticised a speech made by Alderman Davies at a recent Conservative meeting If the money spent en drink, be said, were expended on other articles, we should soon have an improvetuent in trade, and if working-men properly knew their power, and how to nee it, they would never think of giving their votes to a person engaged in that trade. Speak- hag of the Tory candidate for the borough, Mr. Howes said that be was really the faultiest man of all. (Laughter.) Sir Gilbert had been in Parliament, was supposed to be a poli- tician, and should know something about a lot of questions that had been issued with the votes he had given. When asked about it, he said that he did not really remember whether or not he gave those votes. (Laughter.) -lierq, was a member of Parliament, who had served in Parliametit and wanted lobe sent there again, who was so interested is his work that be did not know what he did when he wail there. But Sir Gilbert Greenall said that if he did vote in that way be.was quite wrong, and that he will not do it any more. (Laughter and applause.) Well, it he was wrong ia the past, what guarantee had they that he would be right In the future. If he had such a bad memory he might for:, get these premises, as he had forgot the votes. He was very much like the Yankee who, on one occasion, referring to his political programme, said "That is my programme. If you do not like it, it can be altered." (Laughter.) It used to be said, "Oh that mine enemy would writs a bdolt,'f but he (Mr. Howes) was inclined to alter it in the present case to "Oh that, mice enemy would make a speech." (Laughter.) In a Tory paper ,he (Mr. [fumes) was described as the " ex-umbrena maker." (Laughter.) He pleaded guilty to the soft, impeachment. and prided himself on being able to make an umbrella. When the election came' and the poll closed he might be able to make an umbrella that Would cover all the Tories returned. (Laughter and applause.) In conclusion, Mr. Howes denied that he was a paid lecturer of the National Reform Union, or any other institution, but be took for his profession the study and teaching of politics. (Applause.) He deprecated a lavish introduction of person- alities, his desire being to advocate prit.ciplel in preference to men. Mr. F. ROBERTS proposekl a vote of thanks to Mr. Howes and the chairmm. He thought that the prospects of the Liberals were very healthy, judging from the successful meetings they were holding. Dr."GonNALL seconded the resolution, which was carried with applause, and the meeting then terminated.

Broadbent, Long, Der- byshire, Appleton, Balharry, Blackhurst, John Houghton. A. o.McCorquodale, Greening, J. C. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (valuer), and the assistant overseer. of various town- ships. , . • , Tint ASSBSSMENT OF LAND.—Mr. DARBYSHIRII called lattention to the value of land as compared with other kind of property in the Union. He said that while-15 per cent. was allowed off the value of, other kinds of property, on land there was only an abatement of 5 per cent., and on houses and laud 7i per cent. He had obtained information which showed that in Prescot Union 10 per cent. was allowed off the assessment of land and houses and land, and in Chester and Wirral]. Unions 15 per sent. He (Mr. Derby- shire) thought a larger deduction ought to be made in that Union.—After some discussion Mr. BLACKHIIRST moved, and Mr. GritnEnslNG seconded, that 10 per cent, should be allowed off in the assessment of land and houses and land in that Union; while Mr, Bel-HARRY moved, and Mr. JOHN HOUGHTON seconded, that the abatement be fixed at 15 per cent.—Ultimately it:was agreed, on the enggestion of Mr. BROADBaNT, to defer the matter for further consideration.

This was all the business of public interest.
WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.

A special general meeting of the members of this club was held on Wednesday evening, at the White Bull Inn, Horsemarketetreet. Mr. John Marsh presided, and there was a large attendance.—On the reading of the minutes of. previous committee meetings Mr. J. Derbyshire said that he should like the feeling of the meeting to be tested as to whether they approved of the resolution of committee con- cerning the holding of a monstre demonstration of farmers to agitate in favour of their rights —Mr. T. Stelfox said that the resolution was simply to take into consideration the advisability of holding a demonstration so that the members could make inquiries to ascertain if one would be practicable. If it was found practical to hold one it would take months to arrange—Mr. J. Derbyshire then proposed an amendment to the effect that the part of the minutes under discussion be left out.—Mr. Keowles seconded the amendment.—Mr. W. Darbyslaire supported the minutes, He referred to various letters received from landowners in answer to the rent memorial sent out by the club. He thought that memorial had on the whole been satisfactorily received, and he knew for a fact that several landowners had reduced their rents without further efforts being made on the part of the tenants. He had heard of rents in that neighbour- hood being reduced 10,20, and 25 per cent., and he thought they m ght congratulate themselves on having to a certain extent been instrumental in obtaining those reductions. (Hear, bear.) He should also like to refer to letters received with regard to the assessment of land as compared to house. property in the various Unions in the district at the club. One was from the clerk of tbe Warrington Union, who said that the subject of assessment was a wide one, and that the writer of the paper read to the mem- bers of the club had only touched upon the fringe of the question. He should Le pleased if someone would propose that Mr. Sutton he asked to read a paper to the club touch- ing something more than the fringe. He wee sure Mr. Sutton would readily accede to the request.—The minutes were then passed, the amendment being lost, and it was further decided to make the suggested request to Mr. Sutton.—Mr.Scotrion, of Aigburth (Liverpool), then read an able paper on the land question. He spoke against the laws of primogeniture and entail, which, he said, had no doubt been the cause of the best land of Britain being locked up in the possession of th 6 few. As a consequence, the beat land of the, country had never been in the market for sale, and the twice of other land had been thereby reduced. This tying up of land, he thought; was also the consequence of large towns being overcrowded. Having spoken on the question of tithes, Mr. Scotson said that there were about 600,000 tenants in England. Supposing each was worth about MOO, they would represent a sum of about MO mil- lions. Farmers had been told that they had been well enough represented in Parliament. He thought they had been well enough represented by landowners, but what proper repre- sentation had the agricultural interests had ?' (A voice: "None at ail.") He did not think they had had very much, and that was a subject that demanded grave consideration. He believed that some change was wanted in the mode of managing county business.—A discussion followed the reading of the paper, in which Mr. Davidson urged the members not to lose sight of the necessity for atritating for rent reduction.--Mr. T. Stelfos said that " Yea" bad been answered to most, of the questions put to the Parliamentary candidates for the Altrincham division, but there was some hesitation as to whether farmers should in rating matters be placed on an equal footing with shopkeepers and trades- men.—Mr. John Derbyshire said that if they could not

make themselves beard by appealing to the candidates now offering themselves for election, they must eventually look forward to selecting a candidate to represent their views in Parliament. —Mr. Baxter, Mr. Wm. Derbyshire, and others tosk part in the discussion, after which Mr. Scots m was cordially thanked for his paper.—Tbis was all the busi- ness.

TEMPERANCE FESTIVAL AT WARRINGTON. On Monday evening, a festival of song was given in the Public Hall, Warrington, in connection with the Band of Hope Union. The commodious boiling was packed. A choir of about 300 voices took part, and solos aod recita- tions were given by the Band of Hope children. Mr. R. A. Naylor, president of the Union, occupied the chair, and the arrangements were chiefly superintended by Mr. Frank Williams and Mr. William Roberts, whose active interest in the cause of temperance is well known. Mr. William Crosfield, J.P., Liberal candidate for the borough, notwith- standing the active political campaign he is engaged in, found time to be preseat, and his appearance on the plat- form was the signal for a burst of applause. Mr. C. H. Pigot end Mr. Frank Booth very ably acted as conductor and organist. The meeting was commenced with singing and prayer. The CHAIRMAN then gave an address. He should not, he re- marked, say much to them, as, in addition to the carrying out of an interesting programme, they were to be honoured by an address from Mr. William Croafield. (Applause.) He mast at the commencement congratulate those who bad the management of the entertainment upon the success they had achieved. It must be very gratifying to all the workers in the Band of Hone movement to find such a magnlficent audience assembled, for, to use a popular expression, the hall was packed "from door to ceiling." He should like to take the opportunity of putting right a little matter that he had heard mentioned. It appeared that those connected with the Band of Hope movement could not please everyone, and he understood that some people had taken very great , offence that the advertisement announcing the demonstra- tion only appeared an one of the Warrington papers, and , that all the printing in connection with it bad been entrusted to one firm. It was gathered from that that the Band of Hone Union had something of a poly political :character, but he wished to say that it knew no sect and no party. .(Applause.) It was unfortunate that ail the papers in Warrington had not been favoured with an adver- tisement, and he should have liked to have seen it appear in the cohere as well as in the "Examiner." The Band of Hope movement was, they would he aware. under great ob- ligations to the Press. He was glad to say that he bad been connected with the movement as long as he could remem- ber. There might be things tkat he'might regret having done, and steps he might be sorry to have taken, but be -should always be glad that it had been his very great privi- lege arid honour to be associated with the Band of Hope work. (Applause.) No one could estimate the importance of Bands of Hope, and he hoped that the fathers and mothers present who had children on the platform and in -the body of the hall would encourage them to attend the Meetings regularly. If they would train their children in the way of sobriety—and the best way to do it was by setting them a good example—they might depend upon it I that after they were dead their children would call them blessed. (Applause.) They were engaged in a noble Work. It' was a grand thing to rescue a drunkard, but it was a nobler thing to prevent a boy or girl ever treading in the drunkard'e downward footsteps. He hoped that they would all be still more in earnest in encouraging and promoting the good came, and they must be determined t hat "Come what will, we will dare, and we will do, whatever must be done' until for this grand old cause of truth the victory shall be won." (Applause.) Ma. WILMA( ditoentan, who was received with loud and continued applause, said that in these days, when there was the noise of party strife out of doors it was a very pleasant thing for those who were driven-by circumstaoces to live so much in the noise ef battle to come to a gathering like that, and hear the sweet-voiced polit clans who had just been singing what was their will concerning the curse from which so much suffering came. (Applause.) It was very pleasant, he repeated, to hear so many sweet voices united in harmony, and he was told that the platform was not big enough to hold all the friends whe would be glad to join. It Was pleasanter atilt to face an audience like that, where lane felt assured that everyone was there with the in- tention of harmoniously ocanbiniog against one foe. They were called bigots, and if to be a man of one idea, and to be determined that everything one did should tend to make one's fellow citizens happier, one would be well content to be called a bigot. (Hear, hear.) But teetotallers were bigots, he thought, rattier in the sense that they were all united, all s 'parties and sections of the great church, all parties and ,politics, were united on the common platform of temperance to effect the objects which they had so much at heart. (Ap- planse.)' But that was rather a meeting of hope. There was one line in the second song that had had been sung, "And men are losing heart," that he did not think was exactly in p'sce at tlait meeting: There wall much to discourage them, much misery around them which they could not single- handed Cope with, bat they were a band of hope. (Ap- planes.) They were not looking so much on the past as at ; the future and the young people there were going to see a brighter England than the elder ones had seen, because they were hopeful of the success Of that great movement The Band of Hope had done very much in the past, but things were brighter to-day than they were five and twenty years ago, because the children had bees gradually trained in the ways of temperance, and those ways conduced to the ways of righteousness. The children of to-day would be the men and women of the future, and if they could implant in their minds temperauce views and temperance habits, which were greater still, they might depend upon it that there Was a brighter future in store for them. It was time that they should cheer up, and if there was any feeling of despon- dency like that suggested in the line quoted, let it be put away, and let them all go on cheerfully and hopefully, and they should win. (Applause.) He was talking very much like a patriarch—(laughter)— but he had associated with temperance friends for very many years, and many if them were just now indulging in a great deal of jubilation on the celebration of their jubilee of temperance. There was one old veteran, Bir Edward Baines, of Leeds, was on a platform a few years ago when he (the speaker) had the honour to be with him, and he said that he had reached the 49th year of his temperance life. And he almost thought that be might say he also had now almost reached the jubilee of his temperance life. (Applause.) That did not mean that he was a very old man, but it was because With him his temperance life was the name length as his natural life—(applause)—so that they must excuse him if there was anything patriarchal in the tone of his remarks. They no doubt had their days of discOuragement„ as they had innumerable days of pleasure and encouragement is their work. Most of those who had been long in the work knew that they were constantly meet- ing with instances of encouragement, and where twenty years ago they met one such case now they met dozens and scores. (Applause.) Removed very much among people both in public and private life, and one thing often aston- ished him, It was the frequency with which men of middle age, when applying for situations and when the details of their life had to be questioned into and examined, said they were life-long abstainers. (Applause.) This did not come to the surface ostentationsly,and it was only when questiens were asked that it was found out. Life-long teetotalers were in these days by no means scarce, and the Cause was making progress. There was a story told of a pilot on the Miesissippi some years ago. lie was in a great hurry to get down the river te deliver his cargo for the New Orleans market, and was going at a glorious pace. Night Came on and still high speed was kept up, and, as the boat passed down the river the pilot saw a cottage, whence came the sounds of fid,dling. Soon after he passed another cottage in which also fiddling was going on, and the experience was repeated no less than ' six times during the night, much to his astonishment. When daylight came he found that instead of going down the river past a number of cottages, he had got into a whirl- pool and had been going past the same house all the night. I That man raw a landmark, but it did not follow that the landmark meant progress. The teetotalers were more wide- awake, and their landmarks did mean proirress. (Applause.) He was always warm when he went to a temperance meet- ing, and there was no kind of temperance meeting made him so happy than a Band of Hope meeting, because he felt aatisfied that the habits in which the young people were trained were those in which they would in all human pro- bability spend their lives. There might be some parents who were inclined to say that they themselves took a glass of beer and thought it as well that their boys should do 80 also. When the boys came to a full age, they said, they could chose for themselves whether or not to join a temper- ance society. That was not fair. If they gave a child when young a taste for beer they were shutting up one avenue of choice. The principles he had always advocated were that children should be brought up as total abstainers, and when they grew older they would have a fair chance of saying whether they would take drink or do without it. If he had succeeded in implanting that one idea in the minds of that great crowd, be thought he should not have I spoken in vain. (Loud applause.) The programme, which included songs by the children, I with Solos, and recitations, was ably carried out, great credit being due to the conductor, Mr. Pigot, the accompan- ist, Mr. Booth, and Mr, Frank Williams, the energetic sec- rotary. Recitations were given by Mary Hayes, Annie Eland's, Elizabeth Turner, and W. Alford. Solos were sung by Miss Polly Jane,Mies Eulalie Pigot, Miss Louisa Horton, Miss Alice Mills, Miss Podtnore, and Mr. Frank Williams. At the conclusion, Mr. W. Roberto, in proposing a vote of thanks to the chairman, explained with reference to the advertisements in connection with the society mentioned by the chairman, that in every case meetings had been adver- tised in both local papers, but in the present instance the advertisement had not been inserted in one entirely owing to an oversight on the part of one of the officers of the society, no doubt caused by the onerous nature of his duties. He also explained with regard to the printing khat the Union, when it was commenced and funds were low, asked tenders, the result being that one firm, that now appear to feel aggrieved, refused to tender in consequence of theT smallness of tbe amount. In addition to that subscriptions were aeked, and in one cases positive refusal was made, and in the other a generous response was elicited. The corn- mittee had acted with the strictest impartiality, and the de- sire to do what was best in the interests of the society.— Mr. Dell seconded the resolution, which was carried, and '-e meeting terminated.

~. . . CANDIDATURE. '' - • ' MEETING AT BURTON WOOD. ' .. . Colonel McCercitionale Liberal candidate for ,Newton Division, addressed a sneeting of his supporters at Burton- wood Sn Saturday afternoon. A drenching rain was fall- lug, but a fair" nunibeibf the voters of the neighbourhood assembled and gave,the,e,andidate, who is day by day gain- leg Populti, e'cordiarweldome: The'cltair was filled by Mr. Neill (800, and Mr. A.C. McCorquodale; ifP., Mr. G. W. Rawlins (Rainhill), Mr. P. Hall (Earlestown), Mr. Thomas Ilerton'(Collins Omen), and Mr. F. Broadbridge (ildetion agent) Were elan on the' platform. In a brief in- , troduction the Chairman told how the choice of those en. , 'trusted with the selection of a candidate had falletr,on Col. McCorquodaie, whose answers to their questions and ex- position of his political views were so honest and straight- forward, that they thought Sir Richard Cross, the Tory candidate, would have a very poor chance against 'him. (Anplause.) Colonel McCorquodale, who was heartily cheered, then • addreeted the gathering.' Despite, he 'geld, the strenuous opposition of the Tory party, the Liberals 'had :given the people the franchisS--(applause)—which; although tb them rt might be now called a privilege, would to their Children be a birthright. (Loud applause.) • -Mani!' People thought 'there was danger in entrusting the vote to agricultural labourers and working-men, Who, the Tories said, would 'probably be easily led away: Perhaps that, Was Why they were now trying to lead' them astray. (taughteii•ait'l ap- plause.) He had had,a large and satisfactory experienee of the *Thing claisee of this country, and he considered that ' they'were trim:tele to the working-men of the werld, they Imo* how tee Conduct themselves with the greatest propriety, had were illaw-abiding class: (Applause.) The manifesto of Mr. Gladstone he'continued, he at once endorsed;ind. ' ha Was glad to find from* addresses issued within the few ',lays previous, that other candidates for Parliamentary hon- ours took the same course, and identified themselves with the four great issues which Mt. Gladstone considered shonld be brought forward in the ensuing Parliament. The first of those issues was with regard ' to the church, and the next with regard to county -boards. • It was proposed that a change should be made by which County Boards, represen• tatfve and eteeted by- the people, should have control of the rates and various county business that was at present put before Parliament. These matters, he thought, WOUIEI be far better undertaken by people acquainted with the local requirements of districts. He also thought that the power of licensing would be better placed in We hands of such hoards, than in those of the magiatrates. The ',abject of educatiori Was now also a pressing one. He seppOsed"that the present system of educationets conducted in denomina- tional schools would not be disturbed, but he should like some change in 'the manner of assisting those parents who Were unable to,pity school': fees. (Hear, bear.) Speaking tangmfaogrispotroattei'mhte tirl?..gehntarnantted t andw a s as ai)earrypt:aUppLeateal tn before the Guardians; because through varioug unavoidable , means they were unable to pay school fees for their off- . i spring. It occurred to him that it would be s much better plan for the School Attendance Committee to decide suoh cases, which would do away with the idea that it savoured: of pauperiam to go before the Board of Guardians. Ile,did not like the idea, of ' free education, for there was just a chance that they might not get religious education. They would .agree with him that nothing wee more important than traihing children to have•,a knowledge Of the Bible and $9 learn ,their duty, to their neighbours and their Gorl.• 'Tha remarks made by' Sir. R. A. Cross in his election address on the question of free, educa-• tioos did not, he contended, give a proper answer to it. ble• thought a person's opinion on that subject, one of stroll im- portance, should be made as clear as uoonday—(applause)— and contended that he himself had given a plain answer. (Applause.) Speaking of the land question, Mr. McCerquo- dale said that in that neighbourhood there • were enormous. quantities of land lying idle, almost gone to waste, which,' owing to the present laws, could not be sold. The law of primogeniture must be done away with, and the law of entail must be changed, for property should not be tied up for the benefit of unborn children. A person should be at liberty to sell his own property, and a change in that direc- tion would be of benefit to the landed proprietor, the farmer, and the labourer. The House of Lords, he urged, shorild be so constituted that it will not thwart the well-considered measures brought before the House of Commons by the representatives of the people. The people of the country would rule—(applause)--and It was for the two millions of new voters to decide how the country should be governed in the future. He should be sorry to see that House done away with, but thought its constitution should be amended. Having spoken on the question of trade, and on foreign affairs, he expressed himself deeply sensible of the honour done him in their selection of him as candidate for the division. If sent to Parliament he would endeavour to do 1 his duties faithfully, but whatever the result of the contest ' should be he should never forget the honour paid him. (Ap- plause.) '1 Mr. Horton proposed: "That this meeting, being of ' opinion that Colonel sleCorquodale is a sound Liberal, and, acquainted with the requirements of the district, considers' that he is a fit and proper person to represent the Newton, Division in Parliament, and pledges itself to use all lawful, means to scours his return." (Applause.) Had it not been, he said, for the Liberal party, they oould not have met there as voters, but would, as it were, have been dummies. Now they could make their influence felt, and he urged them to ' do so by supporting the Liberal candidate—Mr. William 1 Sephton, in a few appropriate words, seconded the resolu- tion.—Mr. Rawlins, in supporting it, said that the thanks of the country were due to Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party for the extension of the franchise to the counties, and Mr. P. Hall, who also supported the resolution, showed that the Liberal candidate was well qualified to represent the division in Parliament. —The resolution was then carried, with only two dissentients, and the meeting concluded with the customary vote of thanks to the chairman.

The Leicestershire miners, who have been agitating for an advance ef wages, have been met by the mastes in a very oonciliatorY spirit, and the men began working on Thursday at RP advanced rate at 2d per ton, which is equal to au increase in wages of nearly 10 per cent. The concession has given great satis- faction to the men. MURDER IN CHESIMIL—The Coroner fer West Cheshire on Wednesday bald an inquest at Woodchurch on the body of Mary wife of a farm labourer. On Saturday night the couple were quarrelling, and the woman was heard calling out that she was being murdered. Next day the body was found in the house, covered with wounds and bruises, which must have been inflicted with great violence. The husband was arrested, and the jury now found a ver- dict ef " wilful murder" against him. SINGULAR RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—The ten o'clock night express from Crewe to Euston had a narrow escape on Mon- day whilst passing near Norton Bridge, between Crewe and Stafford. One of the engine rods broke and forced its way into the cylinder. causing great leakaeu of steam. The driver and fireman, to prevent being scalded, left the fire- plate—the former riding on the step. He afterwards fell off, but both escaped injury. After considerable delay, another engine took forward the train. SEVERE SENTENCE ON SKYE CROPTERIA—Before Sheriff Blair, at Inverness, on Wednesday, Donald Maclean and Ronald M'Arthur, crofters, were charged with deforcing Mr. Grant, solicitor, at Ell isbadden, Skye, on the estate of Major Fraser, on March 13, while he was serving summonses of removal. • The prisoners, who were respectable-looking elderly men, were found guilty and sentenced te imprison- ment for forty-two days, without the option of a fine. The sentence is considered severe, and has caused some indigna- tion in the north.
