div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON. THURSDAY. The Conservatives have got hold of a good thing' in the cry of "The Church in danger,' and are working it with skill and vigour. Quite a number of Dukes and other respectable Whigs, with Lord Grey at tho head,., have published a manifesto de- - daring that whilst their affection and attachment to Liberal principles remain unshaken, they will not help the party whose ultimate object is to dis- establish the Church.. The Bishop of Oxford has come to the front with a trumpet-toned defiance." "It is," he says, " time for us to say that we do not mean to be dissolved.' Bven and Brabourne, with a delightful uncon- sciousness of the humourous side of his interposi- tion, joins in the fray, and boldly makes reference to the fact that he has " attended many large meet- ings in different parts of England "—meetings at which he omits to say he was impartially howled at by Liberals and Conservatives whose honest liCsgrish spirit revolted against his kind of political

There is both fire and smoke in these demonstra- tions. The Bishop Of Oxford, with something more than episcopal energy, hits the right note when he cries "hands off" to any who would touch the Uhurch. There is no doubt that hundreds and thousands of ordinary stout Liberals will at the coming election either abstain from voting for sup- porters of Mr. Gladstone or will even give their votes on the other side. This would be a course more creditable to their emotions than to, their in- telligence. Nothing can be clearer than that in the coming Parliament the question of the dis- establishment of the Church will not arise. A ques- tion like that can be taken up only: by a Parliament that has been elected on the sharp issue of establish- ment or disestablishment. That is not the question stow before the country, and it is not a question that can be legislated,..upon in the House of Com- mons about to be elected. Nevertheless fears are excited, prejudices are played upon, and the Con- aervatives, more especially that great buttress of the Church, Lord Randolph Churchill, are confidently counting upon-much gain at the polling booths. I think this expectation will not be disappointed, but it will have rather the effect of reducing the majorities of Liberal candidates than of seating Conservatives. I have been privileged to see a list of the prospects of the general election, prepared by a high electoral authority on the Liberal side for the information of the leaders of the party. This is not a bold guess at the issue founded on general- ities. It is an exhaustive:analysis of the probabilities of events in the various constituencies, made with the assistance of local authorities. It is drawn up upon the plan of giving every doubtful seat to the Conservatives, and the net result is to show a Liberal majority of 83 over the united forces of Lord Salis- bury and Mr. Parnell. Looking down the list, in which every constituency of the kingdom is dealt with, I notice that Bath is looked to to return two Lijserals, Gloucester one, Ipswich two, Leicester two, Lincoln one, Northampton two (and they need not be named), Stoke-upon-Trent two, Warrington one, Hanley one, and Bradford three. On the other hand, I regret to see that Exeter is expected to re- turn a Conservative, and Preston two, whilst Shef- field is put down for two Liberals and three Conser- vatives. But, as I have already mentioned, in order not to take too sanguine a view of the situation, wherever a doubt exists the Conservatives receive the benefit of it. As far as the counties are con- cerned, Devonshire is in the black list, being esti- mated to return seven Conservatives against one Liberal. Gloucestershire will send three Liberals and two Conservatives. In Lincolnshire the representa- tion is pretty evenly divided, twelve Liberahl against eleven Conservatives; Leicestershire two Liberals and two Conservatives, Staffordshire four Liberals and two Conservatives; Suffolk is feur to one on the wrong side.- But Yorkshire stands out splen- didly, with the piomise of twenty-one Liberals against five Conservatives. It will be interesting to see to what extent these particulars are verified. But of the great fact that bfr. Gladstone will be re- turned to power at the head of a working majority Olt can withstand a combination of political machination and scarcely veiled sedition there is no doubt in the minds of Liberal authorities. - Everybody in London, and many people out of it, are familiar with the name of Attenborough. It is the great firm of pawnbrokers, who through more than one generation, have hopefully lashed the glitter of the three balls in the eyes of impecuni- ous passers-by. Pavrnbroking, it is well known,is a profitable business, more especially when conduc- ted on the scale and in the style of the Atten- boroughs. In fact in the year 1874 Mr. Richard Attenborough, having acquired a fortune of a hun- dred thousand pounds, retired from business. It might be supposed that having comfortably, inves- ted his money with the sweet simplicity provided by, the three per cents, he would have rested upon his oars and upon the achievements of a moderately long and extremely busy life. That, however, was , not his view of enjoying himself. He immediately plunged into business of a kind of which he pre- sumably knew nothing. He bought coal mines, iron mines, and lead mines, and proceeded to work them. The result was that in June last he found Itimself not only with his .£lOO,OOO sunk in bottom- leas pits, but with liabilities not far short of 'a quar- ter of a million. This remarkable story, which car- Ties a useful moral for people about to retire from business, was yesterday told by Mr. Attenborough ihimself in the seasoned ear of the Registrar in Bankruptcy. The Atlantic Cable brings a plea, of news which recalls a memorable chapter in history. It announces that the Monument to Major Andr6 has been blown up by dynamite. This monument was erected a few years ago by Mr. Cyrus Field, a generous action which at the time led to much controversy in the United States. Major Andr6, every schoolboy will remember, was taken in disguise by the Americans, -who had just declared their country to be "free, .sovereign, and independent." Andre, who was an .-adjutant-general in the British Army, had been in -communication with the American general, Arnold. Whatever Andr6 may have been, there is no doubt 'that Arnold was a double-dyed traitor. He nego- tiated with the British officer for the betrayal of his own cause, and, there is reason' to believe, betrayed his confederate. Andr6 was treated as a spy, and .on the 2nd of October, 1780, was hanged as such. It is on thispoint—, whether Andre should have been treated as a spy or a prisoner of war—that history has wrangled for a hundred years. It is, I think, not generally known that the remains of Andre rest in Westminster Abbey, though I could not find the grave yesterday, nor did the vergers known any- thing about it. Forty years after his death, the remains of Andre were given up by the American government, brought to England, and laid with honour in Westminster Abbey, England treating as a hero the man the United States denounced as a spy. Mr. Cyrus Meld stirred up anew this troubled pool of controversy when, three years ago, he put up the monument which some excited Irish Ameri- cans denounced as an insult to the country, and have now wiped out with dynamite. It is said, but probably it is only an example of the gossip that floats about clubs, that the Prince of Wales is responsible for the high play which is one of the characteristics of social life in -London just now. The Prince, so the gossip goes, will never play a game of whist for less than .C. 5 points, and £25 on the rubber. That is, however, very commonplace kind of excitement compared with some which an earlier Prince of Wales was .accustomed to seek out for himself. I heard the other night a story about the Prince Regent, told by a descendant of one of the actors in the episode. One evening at Carlton House the conversation turned upon the interesting topic of the relative speed of the turkey and the goose over a ten mile span. The conversation was introduced by a Col. Hanger, one of' the Prince Regent's boon com- panions, to whom suspicion subsequently attached of having arranged a put up job." Finally a match was arranged for twenty geese and twenty turkeys to go a distance of ten miles, the start to be made at five o'clock in the afternoon. Hanker backed the geese, the Prince Regent and most others at the tables backed the turkeys, who cer- tainly seemed better qualified for winning. But Hanger knew what he was about, as the sequel proved. It was in the summer, the days beginning to grow dark towards eight o'clock. The strange procession marched along the road, the turkeys plainly winning by many necks longer than their own. As soon as the shades ot evening began to gather in, " however, the turkeys, finding close over their heads the outstretched branches, strained their necks, , flew up to roost, and there remained for the night, whilst the geese plodding along came in the winners. Colonel Hanger potted a large sum, and the Prince Regent had not been so disconsolate since therWalcheren expedition.

SIR GILBERT GREENALL'S NONSENSE.

Sir,—On reading your report of the flimsy speech given by Sir Gilbert Greenell, the Tory orator, at one of his ward meetings last week. I observe that he made a grave accusa- tion against the Liberal party with regard to toe election of 1880. Briefly put, he asserted that Mr. McMinnies might have been unseated by petition, presumably for bribery, but such petition was not made becausa the Coneervative party had themselves been guilty, and would have gained nothing. Sir Gilbert makes a charge which Ido net think he could prove, and in the same breath admits the guilt of his own supporters. Which party, therefore, stands in the best position? The one charged, and probably in- nocent, or the one admittedly at fault? The answer is patent. It is a pity that the ancient brewer should make such woef-.1 statement, and then plaintively complain that someone is laughing at him, but it will do no harm to the party he derides. It will rather do good to the cause of his opponents, for the electors want from one who asks their suffrages good sense, and not milk and water pabulum. . —Yours. dm., WALTON.

Slit G. GREENaLL AND TRADE. Sir,—At every meeting of the Conservative party, Sir Gilbert comes torward, and in his own peculiar style. " with 'bated breath' and whispering humbleness," profanes his undying love for the working-men of this borough, and his fatherly sympathy with everything which concerns them. It is entirely a matter of " Codlia's yoer friend, not Short." It would be well, however, if some of these working-men, particularly in the building trade, asked the candidate where the contract for putting up the new " Roebuck " public- house in Bridge-street went to. One would also like to know to what extent the trades- men of this town are patronised in the way of articles , in daily use and consumption in a mansion such as Walton With regard to the ship canal I do not remember seeing Sir Oilbert's name on the list of subscribers during the great struggle for the passage of the bill. On the other hand, I believe he told us the Ship Canal would go "into his vitals." In connection with the passing of that magni- ficent scheme we have nothing te thank Sir Gilbert Green- all for. It is well sometimes to examine these claims for popular support, and to note the foundation en which they rest.—Yours, &c, 14ELIX HOLT. Nov. 3rd, 1885.

div.head: LORD R. CHURCHILL AND. THE IRISH.
div.p: LORD R. CHURCHILL AND. THE IRISH.

Sr.—l wish to point out to the Irish electors, and all who have any sympathy with the Irish cause, how Lord R. Churchill spoke of the Irish when Mr. Meldon proposed to Put the franchise in Ireland on the same terms as in Eng- land. On February 14th, 1879, in the debate in the House a Commons on Mr. Meldon's resolution, the noble lord used these words :—" The enthusiastic audiences of Meath (Mr. Parnell), Cavan (Mr. Biggar), Mayo (O'Connor Power), and Dungaryan (Mr. O'Donnel) were composed almost .-n- -tirelv of the ignorant, idle, and drunken, Oh.') The most mad and scatter-brained policy ever conceived by MA found its sole adherents in the Irish who. had no votes, and to whom it was now intended to give votes. He wished to establish this fact, 'The utter incapacity of the anenfranchised classes to decide political problems." The extension of the borough franchise to Ireland would be pro- ductive of the most mischievous and deplorable results.'" Whilst this language was being cheered by the Tory party, the Liberal party—especially Mr. Bright, Mr. Cham- berlain, and Sir C. Dilke—were advocating and supporting the proposal for enfranchising the people of Ireland. We therefore earnestly hope that the Irish electors in Ireland and England will be true to their best and truest friends.— Yours respectfully, EDWIN WRIGHT. NOV. 5,1855.

THE ALLEGED POACHING AFFRAY AT FRODSHAM. Sir,—Permit me to pass a few remarks concerning the ' questionable character of the sentence inflicted by the magistrates on the defendants in the above case. The whole thing from the first has been a curious concern. In the first place it could not be said that the prisoners were tres- passing in pursuit of game, for when discovered by the police they were on a pathway used by the public. In such a place the police exceeded their power by interfering with them. And again: when they were searched no game was found in their possession, for surely rabbits cannot ba justly termed game. But our local magistrates, whenever they fancy the Game Preservation Act has been in the least in- fringed, are guilty of stretching that Act to its utmost dimensions. lam pleased to see that the Liberal candidate (Mr. Irwell) expresses in his address to the voters a desire on his part for a reform in the existing magisterial system ; and I trust that every intelligent workiog-rnan and farmer who possesses a vote will be able to distinguish friends from foes. Hew can we with reason expect that our magistrates —who for the most part have "vested interest" in the land —will ever enact laws beneficial for the farmers, when by so doing they would lessen in a proportionate degree their own interests and influence. By the way, our bench of magistrates for this division are, I think, all good Canserva- Lives, and ardent supporters of Mr. Tollemache.—l beg to remain, sir, AN OBSERVER. Frodsham, Nov. 3rd.

div.head: LITTLE BIT OF SIR R. A. CROSS.
div.p: A LITTLE BIT OF SIR R. A. CROSS.

81r,—The following is taken from a London newspaper, and may be of interest to the electors of the Newton Divi- sion :—" When the London Committee for the suppression of the traffic in girls endeavoured to bring that notorious trafficker, Mrs. Jeffries, to justice, they were forced to spend £250 in the attempt, with no better result than getting her condemned to the nominal punishment of a fine of £2OO Now, in proceedings of this nature it is usual, if not invariable, for the Government to allow the amount of the fine towards the expense of the prosecution. The Lon- don Committee therefore applied for the grant of the fine before the late Government left office, and again when the present Governmant came in. After several months patient waiting the last appeal of the solicitors acting for the com- mittee elicited the following reply from the Home Office, dated Whitehall, October 13,1885: ` Geatlemen, with refer- ence to the memorial presented by you to the Lords Com- missioners of the Treasury, and which has been forwarded by their lordships to this department, praying that the fine fine of £2OO levied upon Mary Jeffries on her prosecution by the London Committee for the Exposure and Suppres- sion of the Traffic in Bnglish Girls for Continental Prosti- tution might be applied towards payment of the coats and expenses incurred in the prosecution, Jam directed by the Secretary of Stite (Sir IL A. Cross) to acquaint you that be has informed the Lode Commissioners of the Treasury that he cannot recommend the payment of anv portion of the fine as requested in that memorial.—l am, gentlemen, your obedient servant, B. Leigh Pemberton.'" So much for Sir B. A. Cross's answer. This is the gentle- man who likes talking about Christianity. One has well said: "Ii it a wonder there are so many Atheists ? " Such a man ought to be dismissed at once from the service of a country that calls itself Christian. This is the gentle- man who instituted the proceedings against the authors of the Criminal Law Amendment Act,—Yours, Nov. 3rd, 1885. PURITY.

div.head: ENGLAND'S FUTURE.
div.p: ENGLAND'S FUTURE.

- - - Sir,—Sir G. Greenall, in the address he has Fast issued, says "I come before you, as I have always done, in the Conservative interest, and as a member of the Conservative party. which, while following the broad lines of our old popular Constitution, is always ready to support such changes and modifications as the altered circumstances of the times, and the changed condition of the people, may require." On reading the above strangely worded and veiled sentence I felt constrained to ask where, oh! where, in our past history has "our old popular Constitution " shown any breadth? Was it when Mr. Disraeli denounced Sir R. Peel as "a man who never originates an idea; a watcher of the atmosphere; a man who takes hie obeerva-, tions, and when he finds the wind is a particular quarter 1 trims his sails to suit ;" and when he declared that "such a man may be a powerful minister, but he is no more a great statesman than the man who gets up behind a carriage is a great whip ?" Was it, when in the debates of the session of 1845, Disraeli spoke of the Conservative Government as "an organised hypocrisy ?" surely the long experience of Sir Gilbert Greenall ought, ere this, to have opened his eyes to the truth of the last- quoted words of Mr. Disraeli. Wherein, during the past five years, have the Conservative party given to Her Majesty's advisers that patriotic help and advice so neces- sary for the well-being of the country? Each opportunity that offered itself was_ laid hold of for obstructing and hindering legislation. Lord Beaconsfield, in his famous manifesto, stated that "a danger in its ultimate results scarcely less disastrous than pestilence and famine" threatened Ireland, and yet measure after measure intro- duced by Mr. Gladstone, intended and framed as means of rendering justice to Ireland, was obstructed and denounced in language that has only found its climax in the recent utterances of Sir Frederick Milner. Yet what has been the result of this legislation ? Sir W. Hart Dyke stated in the House of Conarnons that the present state of Ireland was eminently satisfactory. I have often wondered whether Sir Gilbert reads the speeches made by members of his own party. Lord Randolph in his address to the Woodstcek electors in 1880 said: "The party led by Mr. Parnell, whieh has for its object the disintegration of the United Kingdom, must be resisted at all costs." If Sir Gilbert holds this opinion, how is it that he, Sir R. Cross, and the American- born Asbmeati Bartlett, so studiously avoided any mention of the subj.ct of Ireland at the recent Tory meeting at the Public Hall? We know the answer to this; it is given to us by every Conservative in quiet conversation :"Stay till the Tories get in ; and you'll see what they'll do for Ire- land."
yJ

The Conservative has not been converted to a sense of truth and justice to Ireland. The best friend Ireland has day, Mr. Michael Davitt. in a recent speech displays a thorough:koowledge of the Conservative character. He says —"For my part I would as soon expect honey from a basilisk. or justice from a Castle judge, as expect good for Ireland from the party of home destroyers, the evictors, the heredi- tary opponents of progress in every country. There was no ' man in the House of Commons who dogged the course of the Land League so fiercely, with the instinct of a sleath , hound, as that political juggler, Churchill, who was descended on the one side from the greatest scoundrel that ever fiaured in the record of British infamy, and on the other side inherited the name and reputation of Lord Castle- reagh, who hounded on the Government to more stringent coercion." These are strong words, but history proves their truth. Enough of the past, yet how shall we judge of the future, by its records? What has Sir Gilbert to say respecting Ire- and? So far as his address goes, all is blank. How is this? Does he believe with the late Lord Beaconsfield,

THE ALTRINCHAM DIVISION. MR. I. S. LEADAM AT CHEADLE. On Friday evening last week, Mr. Leadam ad- dressed a large meeting of the electors of the Chea- dle district in Depleach Hall, Cheadle. The room was crowded, and the interval of waiting for the candidate's appearance was beguiled by the singing of Liberal election songs. Mr. Leadam's appearance on the platform, followed by his supporters, was the signal for loud cheers. Mr. G. F. Fisher presided, and on the platform were Professor Hopkinson, Liberal candidate for East Manchester; Rev. J. W. Paull; Messrs. James Watts, William Fisher, S. D. Stone, R. B. Tatton, W. Mosley, J. Herbert, Milne, William Roughton, J. D. Milne, R. Hodgkinson, &c. ,On the platform were Mrs. Leadam and several other ladies. Mr. Leadam, who was greeted with loud cheers, said his Opponent said he was anxious the farmer should have per- fect security and fall compensation, but he wandered if any farmer bad Wilted the question how he proposed to give that perfect security and full 00mpe03ati0n. fie (Mr. Leadam) had made no concealment about his proposals, but over and over again, at Bucklow Hill, and in a speech be had ad- droned to the North Cheshire Farmers' and Market Gar- deners' Association, he had exhibited his hand, and had pointed out the measures which must be adopted to attain the end they had in view. Ile could not discover any utterance on the part of his opponent, nor any indicatien how he would adopt practical measures for attaining that fall and perfect security he professed to bays so dearly at heart. For 50 years the farmers had listened to professions of that sort from Conservative candidates, but they had never yet had any practical realization of them. (Cheers.) The only way in which full and perfect com- pensation and absolute security could be obtained was through an independent tribunal like the land-court There had been dispersed through the constituency a paper of wonderful length containing a list of so-called " Tory Reforms." (Laughter.) That paper reminded him of a story in the comic history of Sandford and Merton. A Rev. Mr. Barlow—no relation, by the way, of his friend who was standing in the Liberal interest for the Knutsford, Division—(laughter)—kept an academy for young getlemen. He was a gentleman of somewhat convivial habits, and was accustomed to carry about with him prospectuses of his academy with gummed backs (laughter)— setting forth the advantages to be derived by a resid- ence in his academy. (Laughter) When he was in a more than usually jovial condition, the Rev. Mr. Barlow, being no respector of persons would lick the gummy back and apply a prospectus to the object before him—(laughter)—whether it was the bald pate of an old gentleman in front of hiss— (laughter) —or a barn door. (Laughter.) That was the history of these " Tory Reforms." (Laughter.) Their Conservative friends kept a supply of these gummy back labels "Tory Reforms" in their coat tail pocketa—(laughter)—and as sose as they came across my reform, no matter if they had resisted it for a number of years, nor if it had been carried by Liberal majorities. ' out came a label and they were dubbed "Tory Reforms." (Laughter and cheers.)— A motion declaring Mr. Leadam a fit and proper person to represent that division in Parlia- ment was passed with only about half a dozen dissen- tients. MR. I. S. LEADAIsf AT BAGULEY. A well attended meeting of Mr. Leadam's (the Liberal candidate for the Altrincham Division) suppofters was held on Saturday evening in the School Rooom of the Congregational Chapel, Baguley. The Chair was occupied by Mr. J. Lambert, who was supported by the candidate, Messrs. G. Rooke, F. Milne, J. W. Williamson, and Rensitow. Mr. Leadam, who was well received, said he was not a member of that party whose action was invariably to shut its eyes to the existing grievances of the people, and who bad never done anything for the benefit of the working classes. (Applause.) It was by practical acquainance with the neado of the people that they were enabled to remedy the existing grievances, and it was on that ground that he justified himself, if any justification were necessary, in seeking to make their acquaintance with the view of learn- ing, if he could, where the shoe pinched. .(Applause.) Their Coneervative friends were very fertile and profuse in their premiees with regard to the kind of reforms they were going to bring about, and those present would observe on reading his opponent's address that Mr. Brooks assented to a large number of reforms which he (Mr. Leadam). hail laid before his constituents. (Laughter.) But although they would find that Mr. Brooks assented to a number of very useful reforms, they would find a coe- seicuous absence of any practical suggestions how those re- forms were to be carried out. (Hear, hear.) There was one reform which figured largely in his opponent's address. They woulit all, no doubt, have read Mr. Brook's speeches, and have noticed that he had made frequent allusions every- whereto the Act which was known as " Lord Cairn's Act." whtch was- passed without opposition by the present Parlia- ment during the last Ministry. That Act had for its object an easier transfer of land, so as to enable the °weer to sell where he was previously unable to do so. He had nothing to say against that Act, except that it did not go far enough. He wanted to see a reform which would bring shoat a transfer of land which would be beneficial to the whole community. and he felt that it was a question of importance both to the farmer and the agricultural labourer. (Applause.) He could wish to see a system of cheaper and improved transfer, which would not only benefit the land-owninc class, but the people generally. (Applause.) He was unfortunately a Liberal, and there- fore, his first efforts would he not to improve the Position of men of property, but to relieve the grievances and to add to the security of the poor. He was not in favour of bad farming, but of good. Whatever his opponent might say on that matter, he would have to march in concert with his Coneervative leader. The Conservative leader did net propose compensation; it was proposed by Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.)—A. motion pledging the meeting to do its utmost to return Mr. Leadam at the election was passed unani- mously.

WIFR MURDER AT WOLTERAAMP'SDN. On Thurs- day morning, a brutal wife marder was com- mitted at Wolverhampton. The murderer is John Davies, 52, pattern-maker, Gough•street, Blackenhall. For several years Davies has been a heavy thinker, and has been a con- stant terror to his wife, who at last left him and supported herself by chafing. On Thursday morning, about half- past eight, Davies went to the h.mse of P.C. Milburn. and said, "I have come to give myself up; I have finished her." At that time the officer was in possession of a warrant for Davies' arrest for using threats towards his wife, and he im- mediately arrested him. Prisoner further said, "1 knocked her about with a big poker. I have told her 20 years ago that she would bring me to an untimely end." The officer inquired where the mbrdered woman was, to which the prisoner replied, "In St. Luke's Church Schools." Proceed- ing to the schools, which were only a short distance away, with his prisoner, the officer foand some twenty persons gathered together in the boys' school attending to Davies's wife, who lay on the floor in a pool of blood. The poor woman's head had been battered in a terrible manner, and a heavy poker which was found in the same room bore traces of its having been the weapon employed. The woman was almost dead, and in a few moments she expired in the arms of a surgeon who had been summoned by the neighbours. It seems that Mrs. Davies was on Thursday morning busy cleaning the schools when her husband entered armed with a poker, and at once commenced a brutal attack. Davies's wife was younger than himself, and the police state that she belonged to a most respectable Stourbridge family, and had always borne an excellent character. Prisoner was on Thurs. day brought before the Bench and remanded.

RAILWAS ACCIDENT.—On Wednesday forenoon the ex- press from London to Aberdeen ran into a goods train which was drawn up at Bridge of Dun station, between Brechin and Montrose. The stoker and guard of the ex- press, together with two passengers,were somewhat seriously hurt, and great datnage was done to rolling stock. TH CIIMBERI awn BIIROLARY.—The Queen has sent a mese ...ge to Mr. Dunne, chief constable of Cumberland, ex- pressing deep regret at the murder of Constable Byrnes and inquiring as to the condition of the other officers. -The in- jured men are progressing favourably. Nothing has yet been ascertained regarding the whereabouts of the fourth man, for whom an active search is being made. Three of the men in custody for the burglary and murder in Cumberland last week were on Thursday identified by Inspector Roche. The police are believed to be on the track of the man still wanted.

"We are all of no short-oighted ; and, therefore, the fewer promises the,better." What has he to say respecting Free Trade versus Fair Trade? Absolutely nothing,but whata little juggling would enable him in the future to escape from. Sir Gilbert has little respect for his supporters, or the plain— tive wail of "Telemachus" in your Tory contemporary. that he would explain his views respecting Fair Trade, Free Education, and the Land Question would have been re- sponded to. I ask electors to read Sir Crilbert's speech at the recent demonstration. Did ever, from a would-be , politician emanate such miserable nonsense. Captain Reynolds must have felt his position a sore one. To have 'an old man swinging his arm about like a village pump, talking of nothing but" congratulations" and " rejoiciags " must have been trying to the nerves, but how much more trying to the patience of his audience, who were waiting ex- pecting to hear hie political opinions. Surely a gentleman so intimately connected with the land as Sir Gilbert ismust have some matured idea as to what its future must be. ' " Telemachus" must have gone home from the meeting with sore misgivings as to Sir Gfibereemental qualifications te sit in the Rouse of Commons; buttercups are sort" stuff to feed on. But what of the future? Warrington is called upon to do her duty ; England's future prosperity depends largely upon the course her sons take at the coming electiom The tnpire must be preserved intact. This can only be done oy just laws, wisely administered To this end Mr. etosfield says, in his address :--*1 I am, therefore, in favour of grant- ing to the sister isle the greatest possible measure of self- government."' Nowhere in Sir Gilbert's address does the counterpart to this exist. Irishmen, mark this; the man 1 you are asked to vote for does not even condescend to notion you. Sir Gilbert, in the inane speech I have referred' to, raid: "If I knew myself at all, I have no particle of cowardice about me." Sir, I charge not only him, but the whole of 'is party with cowardice, and that of the meanest kind. I charge them with using ambiguous language respecting Ire- land and Fair Trade. They have printed and circulated amongst the workmen at Bewsey the speech delivered by Mr. Pearson at the Pub. lic Ball. Dare they appoint a Tory working-man, or say two Tory working-men, to go along with myself and ano- ther to question Mr. Pearson and Sir Gilbert on Fair Trade, to ascertain how far these gentlemen are willing to go towards Fair Trade, and which of the devious paths they are willing to tread. Mr. Cr...afield has given his opinion on Fair Trade; it occupied nearly two columns of your paper. Where is Sir Gilbert's opinion, and what is he pre- pared to vote for? Ambiguous language is a sign of cowardice CLIFFORD DIX. October 28, 1885.

POPULAR CONCERT.—On Tuesday evening next, a popu- lar concert will take place in Frodsham Town Hall. No effort or expense has been spared to make the concert an entertaining and enjoyable One. VOLUNTEER SUPPER AT FRODSHAIL—A eubstantial supper was given to the members of the I company of the 2nd C It V., in the Town Han, Frodsham, on Saturday evening, by the officers of the company. After the cloth had been removed, the chair was taken by Major Ashton, when Ole usual loyal and patriotic toasts were duly honoured, and the proceedings were enlivened by selections by the band and songa by various members of the company. DEATH AND, FUNERAL OP THE LATE MR. JOHN CHAL- LONER.—OR Sunday, the death of Mr. John Challoner took I place, at Netherton, after a abort illness. The deceased was assistant overseer of Frodsham Lordship, and previous to his electioe to that office was Guardian of the Poor for some years, and at the time of his death was waywarden for the Lordship of Frodsham. He was most energetic and attentivein looking after the intereoas of his township, was held in high esteem by the ratepayers, and had their entire confidence. The deceased was interred at Overton Church on Wednesday, and every respect was shown by the trades- men and inhabitants of Fredebam as the solemn procession passed through the town. The funeral arrangements were 'satisfactorily carried out by Mr. W. Youd, of the Bear's Paw Hotel. Frodsham, who also supplied the hearse and four mourning coaches. FANCY FAIR AT WARRINGTON. - On Tuesday afternoon a Fancy, Fair was opened in the Drill Hall, Warrington, the object Of its' promotion being to raise money in aid of the building fund of St. James's Schools, Latchford. Sir R. A. Cross, *MP., formally de- clared the bazaar open, and amongst those present at the ceremony were the Rev. F. dieter (vicar of St. James's) and Mrs. Slater, the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington (Alderman and Mrs. Harrison), the Rev. Canon Sharp, the Rey. Canon Greenall, the Rev. E. D. Garven, and the, Rev. M. Stephensee ; Lady Greenall acd Lady Brook.; Mrs Quekett, Mr. and Mrs. Beaumont, Dr. Mackie, Mr. and Mrs. Robert Davies, Mrs. P. Stubs, Mrs. Parr, Mr. and Mrs. C. Broadbent, Dr. White, Mr. H. Stanton, Alderman and Mrs. Pickmere, Mr. and Mrs. ,J. White, Mrs. Dun, Mr. and Mrs. H. N. Houghton, Mr. William Sharp. Mr. and Mrs. A. Thomas, Mr. and Mrs. J. Pierpoint, Mr. and Mrs. Matson, Mr. W. H. Brook, Mr. W. Tinsley, Mrs. Wil- kinson Mrs. Buckton, Mrs Armitage, Alderman Chandley, Mrs. Wil- kinson, Mr. and Mrs. J. Bolton, Mr. Joseph Taylor, Mr. T. Hutchinson, Mrs. Venn, Mr. W. Abrahams, Mr. J. T. Picton, etc., etc.—Prior to the opening of the Fair, The Rev. F. &Aran, addressing those present, said that for many months they had been working bard to bring about the result now attained. They were by holding that Fair endeavouring to raise the balance of money necessary to provide for the new schools, the need of which was recognised by every one. The Government had told them that they refused to give any grant unless sonething was done to make the school building better, and the accom- modation was so insufficient that they had to turn children from the doors. There were two courses open to the cem- mittee, one to refuse to build, which would have meant a school Board for Warrington and Latchford, and the other to try and raise the necessary funds. They were perfectly unanimous in choosing the latter alternative. It was per- haps a good motive to prevent another rate being saddled upon their already somewhat over-burdened. pockets, but it was still better to try and ensure for their children religious education in day schools. (Applause.) He believed that that was the great reason why they were striv- ing so hard to raise the necessary funds. Some people thought that if religions education was banished from the day schools it could be easily supplied by more efficient Sunday schools, but his experience led him to believe that children were batter taught as to religious matters in day eohools than they possibly could be in Suuday schools. Mr. Lyon, of Appleton, had given them a magnificient piece of land, centrally situated and in the middle of the population, as a site for the building, and Sir Gilbert Greenall—(applause)—then made his generous offer, given conditionally upon their raising the remainder of the money required. (Applause.) He emphatically contradicted the report that they had raised the necessary money, and that the present was a work of supernragation. They required to raise, if possible, the sum of £9OO by the bazaar. Men- tioning those who had laboriously worked for the success of the bazaar, the Vicar said that Mr. H.N. Houghton bad almost lived for the past six weeks in that ball, and had painted all the walls, and, with the exception of one, all the stalls. (Applause.) Mr. H. Houghton, assisted by Mr. James Bowden, had done the building. (Applause.) Mr. Chandley, assisted by his two sons, had worked energetically in painting one stall. (Applause.) He then desired to thank the stall-holdere and all others who had given their assist- ance in promoting the interests of the bazaar. (Applause.) Sir R. A. einem, who wee applauded, said that he had come to a meeting which, in the flood of talk that was now going on, was to him like an oasis in the desert. (Applause.) The fountain before him reminded him of the refreshing waters of peace which he at that moment saw around him, for there those assembled were of one mind and one heart, and were all desiring to do what they could to help forward the good work. (Applause.) They were trying to secure for their children, and for those who came after, the religi- ous education that they believed they should have. (Ap- plause.) He was brought up tinder a great schoolmaster, the late Dr. Arnold, who was very much imbued with the necessity of religious education, and who said, over end over again, "You cannot have education without religion." As their vicar said, Sunday schools were all very well in their way, but they were not enough. None knew that better than the late Dr. Arnold, who always said, "If I have to teach a lesson in geography, I cannot do it properly without teaching religion at the same time." (Applause.) When they found a clergyman and his wife endeavouring to do their duty like men and women, with only one object in view, they were bound to rally round them and help in the good work in which they were engaged. He wished them "God speed," and was sure they would succeed in their undertaking, because they had gone to work in the right way. He had no doubt that the money would be raised, and had pleasure in declaring the bum open.—The Ideyos, in proposing a vote of thanks to Sir R. A. Crone, said that be did not think they could too warmly express their thanks to that gentleman for tearing himself away from the duties in which he was now engaged, and which might materially affect his political existence, to come and open that b team-. He hoped that the bazaar would be successful, and that the money required would be obtained.—Mr. BEAIVONT seconded the resolution. Referring to Sir Richard Cross, whom, he said, they claimed as having once been a townsman, he remarked that they were proud of having such a man amongst them. When Sir Richard Cross lived amongst them there was no institu- tion that wanted and applied for help, to which he did not give assistance. They were exceedingly obliged to him for coming amongst them at such a sacrifice. He hoped that the bazaar would conclude as it had begun by beiog a great success.—Mr. ROBERT Devies, in supporting the resolution, said that he considered it to be one of the glories of War- rington that they had been able, by private benevolence and munificence, up to the present time to keep pace with the demands that education made upon them. (Applause.) In looking round the room he was reminded of the story of a celebrated Scotch nobleman, celebrated not only for his dignity, but for his convivial tendencies. He occasionally went to a certain ale-house, and, as he had no means at testing the time—as watches were scarce and clocks there were none—when he thought be bad stayed long enough he went out of the door and tried to throw his purse over the signboard (Laughter.) As long as it went over he went back, as IS WAS too heavy; but when it lied been depleted until it would no longer fly over the signboard he thought it was time to go home. (Laughter.) He recom- mended that example to them. There were plenty of sign- boards in the room. Let them throw their purses and not leave them until they refused to go over. (Applause ) The resolution haying been carried, the sale was proceeded with. The Fair then being open to business, visitors had an opportunity to inspect the various stalls and their arrange- ments. The stereotyped style whirl,' is largely characteris- tic of bezears WAS in this instance ignored, and the promo. tens succeeded in imparting a freshness and novelty which , was very pleasing. Instead of simply an arrangement of stalls, the Drill Hall had been made to present the appear- ance, not, as is often now-a.days the case, of some foreign market-place Of town, but of a Fair in which many nation., were represented. Bach stall or shop was fitted, handsomely and with taste, to represent some foreign nation, and the fair attendants, to make the illusion more complete, were dressed in the costume of the nation to which they tor the nonce were supposed to belong. The shops were ereeee ted to stand out from the walls, and, being skilfully paintad, and quaintly constructed, were both striking and pretty In appearance. On sale were many articles of interest tial. value, that could not fail to be appreciated by intending customers at the Fair, tispecially when their attractions were enhanced by the attractive dealers, who plied their many I wares with spirit and success. The cestumes were pretty and elicited much admiration. Councillor Taylor; whe did temporary duty as one of the officers of the law, made one think that, after all, a policeman's "lot" is a happy one, and Councillor Hutchinson, who, in his volanteer uniform, represented the army, looked, very soldierly. Taylor, and Garnett. Welsh : Mes- dames Willcocke, Worrell, Pilling, Cooper, and Misses E. White and Green. Swiss: Mesdames Lyon and Useher, the Hon. Mrs. Albany Erskine, Misses Lilian Brooke, Isabel Macrae, Dorothy Lyon, and Useher. Spanish : Mesdames Ficton, H. Houghton, P. Chrimes, and Misses E. Chandley, Auklend, and Spinks. ZiERIOIIS EXPLOSIoN AT A MATCH FACTORY —An alarm- ing explosion occurred in Cork on Wednesday evening, at the match factory of Messrs. Collins and Hastings, Haien Quay. Great alarm prevailed amongst the 400 people employed in the factory, but only one man and three or four women who were in the mixing room were injured, three, however, so severely that their lives are in danger. On Thursday night the Marquis of Salisbury addressed'a large meeting in the Victoria Hall, South London. He understood that Lord Granville had said on Teesday night that he was coquetting with the enemies of Free Trade to put a tax on the people's bread. He would try to put a stop to that calumny. In the words of Lord Iddes• leigh, it was a "downright thumping lie." Of Free Trade as it issued from the hands of its original teacher he was a hearty adherent, but because he cherished the doctrine of Free Trade he demurred very much to the kind of language that was used concerning it, and still more to the extraon-1 dinary additions which were made to the original text. and I which they were required to believe with equal faith. There I was then the questiou of altering the duties in favour of our colonies—that was to say, drawing the colonies nearer te ourselves by abolishing the custom-ho4s's between the two. He did not say it was possible, but it would be a happy thing if they could recognise the unity of the Empire by , destroying the custom-houses between the colonies as much as they were destroyed between England and Ireland. The question of the Church occupied the feelings of the people of the country even more than the question of property. I Why has it come forward? Lord Granville said they had disturbed the sleeping lion. Not only had they the dation- ciations of Mr. Chamberlain, but they had the pledges of 500 candidates for it.

LATEST NEWS.
Sir Frederick Roberta left London this afternoon by the Brindisi nnul en route to India.

The Earl of Ilchester is gazetted Lord-Lieutenant of Dorset in room of the late Earl of Shaftesbury. Several men were injured by an explosion of gas at the Midland Railway Carriage Works, Derby, on Friday. Mr. Justin McCarthy was chosen at the Nationalist Convention at Londonderry, on Friday, to contest that city. Mr. William Abrahams and Mr, John Finncane were en Friday elected Nationalists' candidates for County Limerick
The Gazette states that the queen has appointed Captain, Edward Durand to be assistant Commissioner for delirat- tation of Afghan frontier. . .
A large representative meeting of the farmers of Pem- brokeshire, held at Pembroke, have adopted a memorial to the landlords seekimg a substantial reduction in their rents.
A riot occurred at Lurgan, on Thursday, between Loyal- ists and Nationalists. St. Vincent's Home was stormed, and firearms were used.

While several youths were celebrating the Fifth in a disused quarry at Bakewell, on Thursday, a lighted cracker fell upon some gunpowder, which consequently exploded. Two of the lads were injured. THE MURDER BY BIIRGLARS.—The inquest on the body of Constable Byrnes, killed by armed burglars who were endeavouring to effect tttek escape after robbing Netherby Hall, concluded at Penrith, on Friday. The jury returned a verdict et "Wilful murder" against the three men in custody._ _

THE NEW PARLIAMENT.—The Globe says the new Par- liament will be called together the firet week in January. There will then be an adjournment, and if there is a large Liberal majority, Ministers will at once resign, and a new Ministry will be formed. During the adjournment, if there be a Conservative majority, the programme of the session will be prepared,and if parties are about equally divided the Government will retain office. FATAL FIRE AT PRESTOM—About three o'clock on Fri- day morning a fire broke out at the Birley Arms public- house in Newhall-lane, Preston,. in one of the lower rooms. Mr. Miller (the landlord), his wife, and family, eight per- sons in all, occupied the upper rooms, and their retreat being cut off by the flames, they appeared at the windows shrieking for help. Some were rescued by ladders, others jumped from the windows, but one girl, aged twelve, was burned to death.. Four persons sustained injuries. OPENING OF A NEW BRIDGE RE TRH. QUEEN The Queen drove on Friday front Balin oral to 'falterer, where she performed the ceremony of opening a new four.arch granite bridge over ,the river Dee, erected in the place of the wooden structure which had served to carry the road over the stream since the old bridge was swept away by floods many years ago. At the close of the ceremony. which passed off successfully. Her Majesty, who had evinced keen interest in the proceedings,, drove back to Bal- moral by the south bank of the river..
IHE EASTERN crasls. FIRST MEETING OF THE CONFERENCE.

CONSTANTINOPLE, THURSDAY Evannea—ln his speech at the opening of the Conference to-day, Said Pacha ex- presses the hope that an arrangement respecting the Eastern Roumelian question would be arrived at with the concur- rence of the powers. After the sitting, the Turkish plenipotentiaries visited the Grand Vizier, in -order to ac- quaint him with the day's proceedings. THE TURKISH, WAR PREPARATIONS.

SALONICA, THURSDAY.—Fresh troops- sad furthe r sup- plies of tents, clothing and ammunition have arrived here during the last few days. Evert' available horse and ve- hicle throughout the surrounding country has been requisi- tioned for the transport of stores. Large numbers of troops are being sent to the Greek frontier.

MISS JENNY ADA. WRIGHT, daughter of Mr. Wright, of the Public Hall Hotel, Rylands-street, Warrington, has successfully, passed her examination in music in the junior division and. honours section in the local examination in connection with Trinity College, London. THEA.THE ROYAL.—Am application made by Mr.. Brinsley Sheridan to the borough. magistrates, on Monday, for the renewal of the dramatic license for his theatre in Scotlandhroadi. was granted. WARRINGTON TRADES' COUNCIL.—The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday evening at the Cocoa Rooms, Horsemarket-street, when delegates from the wiredrawers, filesmiths, bricklayers, bakers, and glasscutters were present. After the minutes of last meeting, had been read and passed, a discussion ensued with respect to the urgent ' necessity for workmen ol all. trades to combine to- gether so that the interests of all may be mutually advanced. The delegates were instructed to use their utmost endeavours to, get all trades to unite with. the Council for the common good. 'HALDANE CR/CIPPON AT THE PUBLIC HALL.—On Thursday evening M. Haldane Crichton opened a three night's engagement in the Public Hall. There was a good attendance. The main item in the programme was a special production of Mr. H. J. Byron's favourite play, "sot such a fool as he looks," in which the company have achieved a great success in Manchester: In addition to this item there is the new operatta entitled "Per Parcels Post," and an amusing" moral lesson" to "Husbands and wives." It is needless to say, that . . .

Mr. Crichton's company does ample justice to—these excellent pieces, the opinion of the audience being unmistakeably attested by' frequent applause. A very attractive feature -is provided by the songs which are admirably sang in the course of the en- tertainment. The concluding performance will be given to-night. ENTERTAINMENT AT ST: PETER'S SCITOOL.—The first of a series of entertainments took place in the above schools on Wednesday evening, under the pre- sidency of the Rev. M. Schonberg. There was a large audience. The entertainment throughout was a very instructive and enjoyable one. The first part consisted of the following :—Kindergarten (march- ing and music drill); songs, " Gathered, once more," "He, she, it," children ; song in character, "The careful man," Miss Culm ; song, "Which way," children; pianoforte solo, Miss Place; songs, " Ehren, ou the Rhine,' "Little bird, you are wel- come," "How merry the life of a bird," by child- ren. During an interval of ten minutes, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) made a few remarks, and gave an interesting reading. The second part also mainly consisted of songs, by. the children, but a comic sketch was cleverly gmen by Mr. T. Lawless and Mr. W. Warburton. The children were conducted by Miss Tones; Mr. G. Riley was pianist; and Miss Place also gave solos on the pianoforte. HOLY TRINITY DEBATINe SOCIETY.—On Monday evening a paper on " Popular errors about the Church was read by Mr. H. J. Westbrook at a meeting of this society. The chair was occupied by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton.—Mr. H. J. Westbrook stated that, believing- as he did,it was the bounden duty of all churchmen, rich and poor, small and great—in fact, of all Christians, to make a bold and determined stand against the proposal to rob God of His honour. the State of its religion, and the people of their Church, he offered no- apology for taking that opportunity of contributing his share in that holy and noble work of Church defence. Speaking of the errors about the Church and their origin, he considered that a great and serious omis- sion had been made in the subjects taught in our schools, and especially in those of the Church, in regard to her history, which formed part of the history of our country. Mr. Westbeook proceeded to state that the Church of England waS not estab- lished by Act of Parliament, and that Parliament at some time or other thought it would be to its ad- vantage to set up a National Church, and that the State once made up its mind to endow the Church. lie defied anyone to place his finger on any item in the imperial taxation to bear-out that theory. No disestablishment a the Church would bring about a state of religious equality; and perfect religious equality in the eye of the law was impossible. He denied that tithes were created by Act of Parlia- ment, and churchmen' challenged the production or mention of such an Act. They contended that tithes were the result of the private benevolence of individuals long ages ago, even before there was such a thing as an Act of Parliament; and they further contended that there was, no injustice in the payment of these tithes by people who differed in opuucua from those towhom the tithes were paid. They -were told that the property of the Church of England was national property, and therefore the nation could do as it pleased with it.. Nothing could be easier than to make a statement of that- kind, but the difficulty rested in the proof, and hemust con- fess that he had not as yet seen any proof that the Property of the Church of England was any more national property than was the propertypf the Non- conformists. Mn Westbrook then referred to what was known as Queen Anne's Bounty and the Eccle- siastical Commissioners, and said that neither Queen Anne's Bounty nor the Ecclesiastical Commissioners owed anything to the State beyond its legal con- , stitution. The more he looked into and considered their Church history, the work she has done, the work she was doing, the more firmly did he become attached to her the more he felt it an honour and a privilege to belong to the Church which had such a history, and of which Church the nation's best and noblest men and women had loved to own I themselves members. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks , was accorded to Mr. Westbrook at the conclusion of ; his paper, on the motion of Mr. Calvert, seconded by Mn Radnallo

I desire to say that if any policy-holders de- sirous of information as to the position. soundness, or pros- perity,ot this company, will adopt the proper and imainee.like course of applying direct to any of its agents or superinten- dents, the fullest information will be given.
